docs.title: The AI landscape field guide
docs.text:
About 340 AI and machine-learning terms, explained in plain language and placed on a map of where they sit: pre-training, post-training, fine-tuning, inference, applications.

Made for people who learn from videos and courses and keep meeting new acronyms. Every entry has a short definition and a why it matters line; seven maps show how the pieces fit together.

  • 🔍 Heard a term?

    Use the search box or the A–Z index. Every acronym from the videos is there, including the ones that are only nicknames.

  • 🗺️ Want the big picture?

    Start with the seven maps: the nested circles of AI, the LLM lifecycle, the training loop, the life of one request, inside a Transformer block, RAG and agents, and a decision guide.

  • 📖 Want it explained?

    The glossary has 14 sections ordered like the lifecycle, so neighbours on the map are neighbours on the page.

  • 🛠️ Found a mistake, or a missing term?

    This is a community document. Open an issue or a pull request — see how to contribute.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Thank you for helping make this guide better. The three most useful contributions, in order:

  1. Corrections — a wrong date, number, attribution or mechanism. Open a Correction issue or a pull request, and include a source.
  2. Clearer wording — if an entry did not make sense to you, it probably does not make sense to others either.
  3. Missing terms — an acronym you met in a video or course that is not in the A–Z index.

docs.title: The entry format
docs.text:
Every term in docs/glossary/ follows the same shape. Copy it exactly; the checker and the index generator rely on it.

### Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) { #rotary-positional-embedding }

Today's standard positional scheme: encodes position by rotating the Q and K vectors so attention depends on relative distance.

**Why it matters:** Does not extrapolate well on its own, but can be cheaply stretched to longer contexts (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN), which is what makes 128k-token contexts practical.

<small>*Index aliases:* rotary embeddings</small>
  • Heading: the term as people say it, with a short acronym in parentheses if there is one, and a stable id in { #kebab-case }. Add ★ before the id only for the “learn these first” terms (keep that list to about 30).
  • Also known as: longer expansions, several acronyms, or product names, comma-separated. Optional; use it when the acronym does not fit in the heading.
  • Definition: one to three plain sentences. Say what it is and, if useful, who uses it. Numbers and dates are welcome when they help (“Llama-3-8B has 32 query heads and 8 KV heads”).
  • Why it matters: one sentence, in the reader’s interest: faster, cheaper, more accurate, safer, or “explains why videos say X”. This line is mandatory.
  • Index aliases (optional): extra names that should find this entry in the A–Z index (nicknames, older names, the way a specific course writes it).

docs.title: Style rules
docs.text:
• Plain words first. Write for a strong engineer who is new to ML. Prefer an analogy to a formula; if a formula is needed, put it in the math-notation decoder and link to it.
  • One idea per entry. If an entry needs two paragraphs, it is probably two entries.
  • Place it on the map. Each term belongs to exactly one section; pick the section by when in the lifecycle the term matters, not by how advanced it is.
  • Date what goes stale. Model names, prices, benchmark scores and “the current best” change every few months; say “as of 2026” or avoid the number.
  • No marketing. Describe what a thing does, not how great it is.

docs.title: Fact-checking
docs.text:
• Every date, number and “who uses what” claim in a pull request should come with a source in the PR description (a paper, a model card, official documentation). Reviewers will ask.
  • When you correct something, say what the old text claimed and why it was wrong.
  • If you are not sure, say so in the entry (“widely reported but not confirmed by the lab”). Hedged and right beats confident and wrong.

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/build_index.py     # regenerates docs/index-a-z.md and data/glossary.json
python scripts/check.py           # must print "OK"
mkdocs build --strict             # must build without warnings

CI runs the same three commands on every pull request.

docs.text: Open an issue first describing what the page would show and why the existing maps do not cover it. Diagrams should be SVG where possible (editable, searchable) and must work in both light and dark mode.

docs.title: 1. The big picture
docs.text:
How AI, ML, deep learning and LLMs relate

These are the nested circles of Map 1. Every other term in this guide lives somewhere inside them.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Model ★
docs.text:
A function with learned parameters: input goes in, a prediction comes out. On disk it is a file of numbers (the weights) plus the code that runs them.

Why it matters: When a video says "the model", it means this: a big file of numbers and the program that applies them.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
docs.text:
Umbrella term for any technique that lets computers do things that normally need human intelligence, from hand-written rules to learned neural networks.

Why it matters: The whole field. Everything else in this guide is a sub-topic of it.

Index aliases: AI

docs.title: Machine Learning (ML)
docs.text:
Sub-field of AI where the program learns patterns from examples instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.

Why it matters: Solves problems where nobody can write the rules by hand: recognising a face, judging spam, predicting churn.

Index aliases: ML

docs.title: Deep Learning (DL)
docs.text:
ML using neural networks with many layers. The approach behind modern vision, speech and language models.

Why it matters: More layers let the network learn more abstract patterns (edges → shapes → objects; letters → words → meaning). This is what made today's AI possible.

Index aliases: DL

docs.title: Neural Network (NN) ★
docs.text:
A model built from layers of simple units (neurons) that pass weighted signals forward. Training adjusts the weights.

Why it matters: The basic machine every deep-learning model, including every LLM, is built from.

Index aliases: NN

docs.title: Training vs inference ★
docs.text:
Training adjusts the weights using data: expensive, done rarely, by whoever builds the model. Inference runs the frozen weights to get an answer: cheap, done billions of times, by everyone.

Why it matters: The most important split on the map: stages 3–5 train, stages 6–7 only infer. Prompting and RAG never change the weights.

docs.title: Generative AI (GenAI)
docs.text:
Models that produce new content (text, images, audio, code) rather than only predicting a label or a number.

Why it matters: The shift from AI that classifies things to AI that makes things.

Index aliases: GenAI

docs.title: Large Language Model (LLM) ★
docs.text:
A very large neural network (almost always a Transformer) trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. The engine behind chatbots and coding assistants.

Why it matters: The thing you talk to in ChatGPT or Claude. The central object of this guide; stages 1–7 of Map 2 describe its life.

Index aliases: LLM

docs.title: Foundation model
docs.text:
A big general-purpose model trained once on broad data and then adapted to many tasks. LLMs are the best-known example.

Why it matters: Train once, expensively; reuse everywhere, cheaply. This economics is why a few labs train and everyone else adapts.

docs.title: Frontier model / frontier lab
docs.text:
The most capable models available at a given moment, and the handful of companies that train them (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI, and a few Chinese labs).

Why it matters: "Frontier" in a video simply means "the best there is right now".

Index aliases: Frontier lab

docs.title: Multimodal model
docs.text:
A model that handles more than one data type (text + images + audio + video) as input and/or output.

Why it matters: Lets one model read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, and answer in text. See section 14.

Index aliases: Multimodal (section 14)

docs.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
docs.text:
The field of making computers understand and generate human language. LLMs are its current state of the art.

Why it matters: The older name for the discipline; many pre-2020 techniques (word2vec, BERT, parsing) come from here.

Index aliases: NLP

docs.title: Computer Vision (CV)
docs.text:
The field of understanding images and video. Historically CNNs, increasingly Transformers (ViT).

Why it matters: Where deep learning first proved itself (ImageNet, 2012), and where many terms like "convolution" come from.

Index aliases: CV, Computer vision (CV)

docs.title: Discriminative vs generative model
docs.text:
A discriminative model learns to separate or label inputs (spam / not spam). A generative model learns the distribution of the data, so it can produce new samples.

Why it matters: Tells you whether a model judges inputs or produces outputs. A spam filter is discriminative; an LLM is generative.

docs.title: Narrow AI vs AGI
docs.text:
Also known as: Artificial General Intelligence

Narrow AI does one task well. AGI would match humans across most intellectual tasks; it is a goal and a debate, not a product.

Why it matters: When people argue about AGI timelines, this is the term; nothing you can download today is AGI.

Index aliases: AGI

docs.title: Symbolic AI
docs.text:
Also known as: GOFAI, expert systems

The older, rule- and logic-based approach to AI. Contrasts with learning from data. Still used inside planners and some hybrid systems.

Why it matters: Explains why "AI" in a 1990s product meant if/else rules, and why "neuro-symbolic" means mixing the two.

Index aliases: Expert systems / GOFAI

docs.title: 2. Learning paradigms
docs.text:
How a model learns: from labels, from structure, from itself, or from rewards

Every training technique in this guide is one of these four in disguise. Pre-training is self-supervised, SFT is supervised, RLHF is reinforcement learning.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Supervised learning ★
docs.text:
Learning from examples that come with the correct answer (labels); the model learns input → label. Used in classic ML, in SFT and in reward-model training.

Why it matters: Most accurate way to learn when you can afford labelled examples. Its limit is the cost of labelling.

docs.title: Unsupervised learning
docs.text:
Finding structure in data with no labels: grouping, compressing, spotting anomalies.

Why it matters: Works on data nobody has labelled, which is most data. Finds groups and outliers you did not know to look for.

docs.title: Self-supervised learning (SSL) ★
docs.text:
Supervised-style training where the label is carved out of the data itself, e.g. hide the next word and predict it. This is how LLMs are pre-trained.

Why it matters: Turns the whole internet into free training labels. The single trick that made LLMs possible at scale.

Index aliases: SSL, SSL (self-supervised)

docs.title: Semi-supervised learning
docs.text:
Mixing a small labelled set with a lot of unlabelled data.

Why it matters: Gets most of the accuracy of supervised learning with a fraction of the labelling cost.

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning (RL) ★
docs.text:
An agent takes actions in an environment and learns from rewards instead of labelled answers. Used in games, robotics and LLM post-training (RLHF, GRPO).

Why it matters: Lets a model get better than its teachers: it can discover strategies no example showed it, as long as you can score the result.

Index aliases: RL, RL (reinforcement learning)

docs.title: Agent, environment, policy, reward (RL vocabulary)
docs.text:
The agent is the learner, the environment is what it acts on, the policy is its decision rule (for LLMs: the model itself), the reward is the feedback signal.

Why it matters: Decode any RL video: "policy" = the model being trained, "reward" = the score it is chasing.

Index aliases: RL vocabulary, Policy (RL), Reward (RL), Environment (RL)

docs.title: Exploration vs exploitation
docs.text:
The RL dilemma: try new actions to discover better ones (explore) or repeat what already works (exploit).

Why it matters: Explains why RL training samples several answers per prompt instead of only the best one.

docs.title: Q-learning / DQN (Deep Q-Network)
docs.text:
Classic value-based RL: learn a table (or network) estimating how good each action is in each state. DQN was the 2013 breakthrough that played Atari games from pixels.

Why it matters: The RL you see in game-playing demos. LLM post-training uses policy-based methods (PPO, GRPO) instead.

Index aliases: Deep Q-Network, DQN

docs.title: Monte Carlo Tree Search / AlphaGo (MCTS)
docs.text:
Search that looks ahead by simulating many possible futures and focusing on promising ones. Combined with neural networks (AlphaGo) it beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016.

Why it matters: An ancestor of "thinking longer" in reasoning models: spend more compute at decision time to get better decisions. (Today's reasoning models do it with long chains of thought, not tree search.)

Index aliases: MCTS, AlphaGo

docs.title: Imitation learning / behaviour cloning
docs.text:
Learning a policy by copying demonstrations from an expert.

Why it matters: SFT is imitation learning: the model copies the ideal answers humans wrote. RL is what lets it go beyond them.

Index aliases: Behaviour cloning

docs.title: Transfer learning
docs.text:
Reusing what a model learned on one task or dataset as the starting point for another. Fine-tuning a pre-trained model is transfer learning.

Why it matters: Why you never start from zero: a model that already knows language learns your task from a few hundred examples.

docs.title: Contrastive learning
docs.text:
Also known as: CLIP, SimCLR

Training that pulls representations of matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart (an image and its caption; two views of the same photo).

Why it matters: How embedding models and CLIP learn that "a photo of a cat" and the cat picture belong together.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Predicting a category (spam / not spam, cat / dog).

Why it matters: The most common ML task in business. Next-token prediction is also a classification over the vocabulary.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
Predicting a continuous number (price, temperature, time to failure).

Why it matters: The other basic task; when the answer is a number, it is regression.

docs.title: Clustering
docs.text:
Grouping similar items together without labels (k-means).

Why it matters: Finds natural groups: customer segments, topics in documents, duplicate records.

docs.title: Dimensionality reduction
docs.text:
Compressing many features into fewer while keeping the important structure (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP).

Why it matters: How people draw 2-D pictures of embeddings: hundreds of dimensions squashed down so you can see clusters.

Index aliases: t-SNE / UMAP

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text:
Flagging data points that do not look like the rest.

Why it matters: Fraud, intrusion and fault detection: learn what normal looks like, alert on the rest.

docs.title: Label / ground truth
docs.text:
The known correct answer attached to a training example.

Why it matters: The expensive ingredient of supervised learning; its quality caps the model's quality.

Index aliases: Ground truth

docs.title: 3. Classic ML toolbox
docs.text:
Pre-deep-learning algorithms and the vocabulary of any ML project

Still the right tool for most tabular business data. The evaluation vocabulary here (train/test split, overfitting, hyperparameters) applies to LLMs too.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Linear regression
docs.text:
Fit a straight line (or hyperplane) to predict a number.

Why it matters: The simplest model there is; everything else is a more flexible version of "fit a curve to the data".

docs.title: Logistic regression
docs.text:
A linear model for classification that outputs a probability.

Why it matters: Fast, explainable baseline. If a neural network cannot beat it, something is wrong.

Index aliases: Logistic regression (classifier)

docs.title: Decision tree
docs.text:
A flowchart of if/else splits on features. Easy to read, prone to overfitting.

Why it matters: Humans can read the rules it learned, which makes it popular where decisions must be explained.

Index aliases: Decision trees

docs.title: Random forest
docs.text:
Many decision trees trained on random subsets of data and features, then averaged.

Why it matters: Averaging many imperfect trees cancels their individual mistakes: more accurate and far more robust than one tree.

Index aliases: Random forest (ensemble)

docs.title: Gradient boosting
docs.text:
Also known as: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost

Build trees one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones.

Why it matters: The most accurate choice for tabular data in most competitions and companies. Try this before a neural network.

Index aliases: Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM)

docs.title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
docs.text:
Finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes.

Why it matters: A strong pre-2012 classifier; a wide margin makes it generalise well on small datasets.

Index aliases: SVM

docs.title: k-Nearest Neighbours (kNN)
docs.text:
Predict by looking at the k most similar training examples.

Why it matters: No training at all, just lookup. The same idea powers vector search in RAG: find the nearest embeddings.

Index aliases: kNN

docs.title: Naive Bayes
docs.text:
Fast probabilistic classifier that assumes features are independent.

Why it matters: The classic spam filter; works surprisingly well on text with almost no compute.

Index aliases: Naive Bayes classifier

docs.title: k-means
docs.text:
Clustering by assigning points to the nearest of k centroids and repeating until stable.

Why it matters: The default way to split data into k groups when you have no labels.

docs.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
docs.text:
Linear dimensionality reduction along the directions of largest variance.

Why it matters: Compresses data while keeping what varies most; used to shrink embeddings and to visualise them.

Index aliases: PCA

docs.title: Feature / feature engineering
docs.text:
A feature is one input variable. Feature engineering is hand-crafting better inputs.

Why it matters: In classic ML, good features matter more than the algorithm. Deep learning's big win is learning features automatically.

Index aliases: Feature engineering

docs.title: Train / validation / test split
docs.text:
Data is divided so you train on one part, tune settings on a second and measure final performance on a third the model never saw.

Why it matters: The only honest way to know how a model will do on new data. Skipping it is how projects fool themselves.

Index aliases: Validation set, Test set

docs.title: Cross-validation
docs.text:
Rotate which slice is held out and average, for a more reliable estimate.

Why it matters: Gives a trustworthy accuracy number from a small dataset.

docs.title: Overfitting / underfitting ★
docs.text:
Memorising the training data (great on train, poor on new data) versus being too simple to capture the pattern at all.

Why it matters: Overfitting is the number-one way models fail in production: perfect in the lab, useless on real inputs.

docs.title: Bias–variance trade-off
docs.text:
Simple models err systematically (bias); complex models err erratically depending on the data they saw (variance).

Why it matters: Explains why bigger is not always better: a model can be too flexible for the amount of data you have.

Index aliases: Bias–variance

docs.title: Regularization
docs.text:
Also known as: L1, L2

Penalising large weights to reduce overfitting. L1 also pushes weights to exactly zero.

Why it matters: Makes a model generalise better by stopping it from relying too hard on any one input.

Index aliases: L1 / L2 regularization

docs.title: Early stopping
docs.text:
Stop training when validation loss stops improving, even if training loss is still falling.

Why it matters: The cheapest protection against overfitting: just stop at the right moment.

docs.title: Hyperparameter
docs.text:
A setting you choose before training (learning rate, tree depth, LoRA rank), as opposed to parameters learned from data.

Why it matters: What engineers tune by hand; a wrong learning rate can make an otherwise good model fail completely.

docs.title: Ensemble
docs.text:
Combining several models' predictions.

Why it matters: Usually beats any single model; the same idea as asking several experts and taking the majority view.

docs.title: Confusion matrix
docs.text:
A table of predicted class versus actual class, showing where a classifier confuses things.

Why it matters: Shows which mistakes the model makes, not just how many. Essential when some errors cost more than others.

docs.title: Precision, recall, F1, ROC / AUC
docs.text:
Precision: of what the model flagged, how much was right. Recall: of what should be flagged, how much it caught. F1 balances the two; ROC / AUC summarises the trade-off across thresholds.

Why it matters: Accuracy alone lies when classes are unbalanced (99% "not fraud" is 99% accurate and useless). These metrics tell the truth.

Index aliases: AUC / ROC, Precision / recall, F1 score

docs.title: Data leakage
docs.text:
Information from the test set, or from the future, accidentally reaching the training data.

Why it matters: The classic reason a model scores brilliantly in testing and fails in production.

docs.title: Class imbalance
docs.text:
When one class is far rarer than the other (fraud, defects, disease).

Why it matters: Needs special handling (re-weighting, re-sampling, the right metrics) or the model simply learns to predict the majority class.

docs.title: scikit-learn
docs.text:
The standard Python library for classic ML.

Why it matters: Where almost every tutorial's .fit() and .predict() come from.

docs.title: 4. Neural-network foundations
docs.text:
The training loop and building blocks used by every stage that changes weights

This is what Raschka's book builds by hand. Pre-training, post-training and your own fine-tuning all run the same loop: forward pass → loss → backprop → optimizer step (Map 3).

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Neuron / perceptron
docs.text:
The basic unit: a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.

Why it matters: Everything in deep learning is millions of these wired together; each one is just multiply, add, squash.

Index aliases: Perceptron

docs.title: Weights, biases, parameters ★
docs.text:
The numbers inside the model that training adjusts. "7B" means 7 billion of them.

Why it matters: The parameters are the model. Download the weights and you have it; change them and you have a different model.

Index aliases: Weights (the file), Parameters

docs.title: Activations
docs.text:
The intermediate values flowing through the network for one input (as opposed to the weights, which are fixed during inference).

Why it matters: Weights are what the model knows; activations are what it is thinking right now about this input. Interpretability studies activations.

docs.title: Layer / hidden layer
docs.text:
A group of neurons computed together. Layers between input and output are hidden layers.

Why it matters: "Deep" simply means many hidden layers; each adds a level of abstraction.

Index aliases: Hidden layer

docs.title: Multi-Layer Perceptron / Feed-forward network
docs.text:
Also known as: MLP, FFN

Stacked fully-connected layers. Also the second half of every Transformer block.

Why it matters: The plainest neural network; inside an LLM the FFN layers are where most of the parameters, and most of the stored knowledge, live.

docs.title: Activation function
docs.text:
Also known as: ReLU, GELU, SiLU/Swish, sigmoid, tanh

Non-linearity applied after a layer. GELU and SiLU are the ones used inside LLMs.

Why it matters: Without it, stacking layers would collapse into one straight line. The non-linearity is what lets networks learn curves and complex rules.

docs.title: Softmax
docs.text:
Turns a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1.

Why it matters: How the model expresses "70% sure the next word is 'Paris'". Applied at the output and inside attention.

docs.title: Logits
docs.text:
Raw, unnormalised scores that come out before softmax.

Why it matters: What the model actually computes; softmax just converts them to probabilities. Temperature acts on logits.

docs.title: One-hot encoding
docs.text:
Representing a category as a vector of zeros with a single 1 at that category's position.

Why it matters: The naive way to feed words to a network. Embeddings replace it with dense vectors that carry meaning.

docs.title: Forward pass
docs.text:
Running an input through the network to get an output.

Why it matters: Inference is just a forward pass; training is a forward pass plus a backward pass.

docs.title: Loss function ★
docs.text:
Also known as: cross-entropy, MSE

A number measuring how wrong the output is; training minimises it. Cross-entropy for classification and next-token prediction, mean squared error for regression.

Why it matters: Defines what "better" means. The whole of training is "make this number smaller".

Index aliases: Cross-entropy

docs.title: Backpropagation (backprop) ★
docs.text:
The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the loss, by applying the chain rule backwards through the network.

Why it matters: Tells every one of the billions of weights which direction to move. Without it, training deep networks would be hopeless.

docs.title: Gradient
docs.text:
The direction and size of change in loss for each weight.

Why it matters: The "which way is downhill" signal; backprop computes it, the optimizer follows it.

docs.title: Gradient descent (SGD) ★
docs.text:
Nudge each weight a small step against its gradient. Stochastic gradient descent does this on one mini-batch per step.

Why it matters: The learning rule behind all of deep learning: take a small step downhill, repeat millions of times.

Index aliases: SGD

docs.title: Optimizer
docs.text:
Also known as: Adam, AdamW

Smarter update rules that adapt the step size per weight using running averages of gradients. AdamW is the default for Transformers.

Why it matters: Makes training converge faster and more reliably than plain gradient descent, at the cost of extra memory per weight.

docs.title: Learning rate (LR)
docs.text:
How big each update step is.

Why it matters: The single most important hyperparameter. Too high and training blows up; too low and it never gets anywhere.

Index aliases: Learning rate (LR)

docs.title: Batch / mini-batch
docs.text:
The group of examples processed in one step before the weights are updated.

Why it matters: Bigger batches use the GPU better and give smoother gradients; smaller ones fit in memory. A knob you will see in every training script.

docs.title: Epoch
docs.text:
One full pass over the training set.

Why it matters: Classic ML trains for many epochs; LLM pre-training usually sees each token about once.

docs.title: Training loop
docs.text:
Forward pass → loss → backward pass → optimizer step, repeated. Everything from a toy MLP to a frontier LLM runs this loop.

Why it matters: If you understand this loop (Map 3) you understand what "training" means at every stage of Map 2.

docs.title: Weight initialization
docs.text:
How the weights are set before training starts: small random numbers with a carefully chosen scale.

Why it matters: A bad starting scale makes gradients vanish or explode on step one; good initialization makes deep networks trainable.

docs.title: Dropout
docs.text:
Randomly switch off neurons during training.

Why it matters: Forces the network not to rely on any single neuron, which reduces overfitting.

docs.title: Weight decay
docs.text:
Shrink the weights slightly every step (L2-style regularization).

Why it matters: Keeps weights small, which helps generalisation; the "W" in AdamW.

docs.title: Normalization
docs.text:
Also known as: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm

Rescaling activations so they stay in a healthy range. LayerNorm and its cheaper cousin RMSNorm are the ones used in Transformers.

Why it matters: Keeps training stable in very deep networks; without it, values drift and training diverges.

docs.title: Residual / skip connection
docs.text:
Add a layer's input to its output. Forms the residual stream of a Transformer.

Why it matters: Lets gradients flow straight through dozens of layers, which is what makes 100-layer networks trainable at all.

Index aliases: Skip connection

docs.title: Vanishing / exploding gradients
docs.text:
Gradients shrinking to nothing or blowing up as they flow back through many layers.

Why it matters: The historical reason deep networks did not work before ~2012; residuals, normalization and better initialization fixed it.

Index aliases: Exploding gradients, Vanishing gradients

docs.title: Embedding ★
docs.text:
A learned vector of numbers representing a token, word, image or item so that similar things end up close together.

Why it matters: How a computer represents meaning: "king" and "queen" become nearby points. The input to every LLM and the basis of semantic search.

docs.title: Latent space / representation
docs.text:
The internal vector space in which the model represents meaning.

Why it matters: Where the model "thinks": arithmetic on these vectors (king − man + woman ≈ queen) is what makes them useful.

Index aliases: Latent space

docs.title: Inductive bias
docs.text:
The assumptions an architecture builds in: CNNs assume nearby pixels matter, RNNs assume order, Transformers assume very little.

Why it matters: Explains why CNNs need less data for images and why Transformers need huge data but scale further.

docs.title: Tensor
docs.text:
A multi-dimensional array (vector, matrix, and beyond).

Why it matters: The data type everything in deep learning is made of; a "shape" like [batch, tokens, 768] tells you what is flowing where.

docs.title: Autograd / computational graph
docs.text:
Framework machinery (PyTorch) that records every operation so backprop can be computed automatically.

Why it matters: Why you never write backprop by hand: call loss.backward() and PyTorch does the calculus.

Index aliases: Computational graph

docs.title: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
docs.text:
A network using small sliding filters. The classic architecture for images (LeNet, AlexNet, ResNet).

Why it matters: Detects the same pattern anywhere in an image with few parameters. Still the workhorse for vision on small devices.

Index aliases: CNN

docs.title: Recurrent networks
docs.text:
Also known as: RNN, LSTM, GRU

Networks that process sequences one step at a time with a memory state. They dominated language tasks before Transformers replaced them.

Why it matters: Worked for sequences but could not be parallelised and forgot long-range context. Attention fixed both problems.

Index aliases: LSTM / GRU

docs.title: Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq)
docs.text:
An encoder reads an input sequence, a decoder writes an output sequence (early translation models).

Why it matters: Attention was invented to fix seq2seq's bottleneck of squeezing a whole sentence into one vector.

Index aliases: seq2seq

docs.title: Autoencoder / VAE
docs.text:
Also known as: Variational Autoencoder

Networks trained to compress and then reconstruct their input. The variational version learns a smooth latent space you can sample from.

Why it matters: Learns compact representations without labels; the VAE is also the compressor inside Stable Diffusion.

Index aliases: VAE

docs.title: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
docs.text:
A generator and a discriminator trained against each other.

Why it matters: Produced the first photorealistic generated faces (2014–2020); mostly replaced by diffusion models, which are easier to train.

Index aliases: GAN

docs.title: Diffusion model
docs.text:
Generates images (and audio, video) by learning to reverse a gradual noising process.

Why it matters: The engine behind Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2/3 and Midjourney: start from noise, remove it step by step toward the prompt.

docs.title: 5. Data & tokenization
docs.text:
Stage 1 of the LLM lifecycle: what the model reads, and in what units

Before any training, text is turned into tokens. The tokenizer is built once and frozen with the model, which is why every model counts tokens slightly differently.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Corpus / training data
docs.text:
The collection of text (web pages, books, code, transcripts) the model learns from. Trillions of tokens for frontier models.

Why it matters: The model knows only what was in here. Quality and mix of the corpus decide much of the model's quality.

docs.title: Token ★
docs.text:
The unit the model actually reads and writes. Usually a word piece; roughly ¾ of an English word on average.

Why it matters: Everything is counted in tokens: context limits, speed, and your API bill.

docs.title: Tokenizer
docs.text:
Converts text to token IDs and back. Built before pre-training and frozen with the model.

Why it matters: Explains odd behaviour like miscounting letters in a word: the model never sees letters, only token IDs.

docs.title: Token IDs / detokenization
docs.text:
Each token has an integer ID in the vocabulary. The model consumes and produces IDs; detokenization turns IDs back into text.

Why it matters: The model is a function from integers to integers; text is only at the edges.

docs.title: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
docs.text:
The most common tokenizer algorithm: start from bytes or characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair. Used by GPT and Llama models.

Why it matters: Lets the model handle any string (even emoji and typos) with a fixed vocabulary, while keeping common words as single tokens.

Index aliases: BPE

docs.title: WordPiece, SentencePiece, tiktoken
docs.text:
Other tokenizer algorithms and libraries: BERT uses WordPiece, many open models use SentencePiece, OpenAI models use tiktoken.

Why it matters: Different names in different tutorials, same job: text ↔ tokens.

Index aliases: tiktoken, SentencePiece, WordPiece

docs.title: Vocabulary / vocab size
docs.text:
The set of all tokens the model knows, typically 32k to 200k entries.

Why it matters: A bigger vocabulary means fewer tokens per sentence (cheaper, faster) but a bigger output layer.

docs.title: Multilingual token cost
docs.text:
Tokenizers are trained mostly on English, so other languages split into more tokens per word. Polish text typically costs about 2× the tokens of the same text in English (1.5–2.5× depending on the tokenizer; newer 200k+ vocabularies do better, older 32k ones worse).

Why it matters: The same prompt in Polish uses more of the context window and costs more than in English.

docs.title: Special tokens
docs.text:
Also known as: BOS, EOS, PAD

Control tokens marking beginning / end of sequence, padding, or chat roles (user, assistant, tool).

Why it matters: How the model knows where a message starts and ends, and when to stop generating.

Index aliases: BOS / EOS / PAD

docs.title: Context window / context length ★
docs.text:
The maximum number of tokens the model can take in at once (prompt plus answer): 8k, 128k, 1M.

Why it matters: The model's working memory. Anything outside it does not exist for the model; everything inside costs compute and money.

docs.title: Sequence / sequence length
docs.text:
An ordered list of tokens. Models are trained on fixed-length chunks of the corpus.

Why it matters: "Sequence length" in a training script is how much text the model sees per example.

docs.title: Input–target pairs / sliding window
docs.text:
Training data is cut into chunks; the target is the same chunk shifted by one token, so every position has a "next token" to predict. (Raschka chapter 2.)

Why it matters: How free labels are created from raw text: the text itself is the answer key.

docs.title: Data cleaning, deduplication, filtering
docs.text:
Removing junk, duplicates and low-quality text before training.

Why it matters: One of the biggest levers on model quality: cleaner data makes a smarter model at the same size.

Index aliases: Dedup

docs.title: Data mixture
docs.text:
The proportions of web, code, books, maths, multilingual text in the training set.

Why it matters: Decides what the model is good at: more code in the mix makes a better coder.

docs.title: Synthetic data
docs.text:
Training text generated by another model.

Why it matters: Fills gaps where real data is scarce (maths steps, rare languages) and is now a major ingredient of both pre- and post-training.

docs.title: Data annotation / human raters
docs.text:
People who write ideal answers, rank outputs or label data for SFT and reward models (companies like Scale AI and Surge AI).

Why it matters: The human work behind "human feedback"; its quality shapes how the model behaves.

Index aliases: Human raters, Scale AI

docs.title: Common Crawl, The Pile, FineWeb
docs.text:
Well-known public web-scale datasets used as pre-training corpora.

Why it matters: When a video says a model was trained on "the internet", these are the concrete datasets it means.

Index aliases: Common Crawl, FineWeb, The Pile

docs.title: Chat template
docs.text:
The exact text format (role markers, special tokens) used to serialise a conversation into tokens. Each model family has its own.

Why it matters: A conversation is just one long token sequence with markers; getting the template wrong is a common cause of bad outputs with open models.

docs.title: 6. The Transformer architecture
docs.text:
Stage 2: the shape of the network before any weights are learned

Nearly every LLM is a stack of identical Transformer blocks (Map 5). The terms here describe the parts of a block and the design choices between model families.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Transformer ★
docs.text:
The neural architecture from the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need": stacked blocks of attention plus feed-forward layers.

Why it matters: Processes all tokens in parallel (fast on GPUs) and lets any token look at any other (long-range context). Both are why it won.

docs.title: Attention ★
docs.text:
A mechanism that lets each token look at other tokens and weigh how relevant they are, so context flows across the whole sequence in one step.

Why it matters: How the model knows that "it" refers to "the cat" ten words earlier. The core idea of modern AI.

docs.title: Self-attention
docs.text:
Attention where tokens attend to other tokens of the same sequence.

Why it matters: Lets every word be interpreted in the light of every other word in the text.

docs.title: Query, Key, Value
docs.text:
Also known as: Q, K, V

Three projections of each token. A token's query is compared with every key to get weights, which are then applied to the values.

Why it matters: Think of a lookup: the query asks a question, keys say what each token offers, values are what gets returned.

docs.title: Scaled dot-product attention
docs.text:
The actual attention formula: softmax(QKᵀ / √d) · V.

Why it matters: The one formula every video shows. Dividing by √d keeps the softmax from saturating so gradients stay healthy.

docs.title: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)
docs.text:
Several attention operations run in parallel (heads), each free to focus on a different kind of relationship.

Why it matters: One head can track grammar while another tracks topic. More heads, richer understanding.

Index aliases: MHA

docs.title: Multi-Query / Grouped-Query Attention
docs.text:
Also known as: MQA, GQA

Variants that share key/value projections across heads. Llama 2 (70B), Llama 3, Mistral and most 2024+ models use GQA.

Why it matters: Shrinks the KV cache several-fold, so inference is faster and cheaper with almost no quality loss.

docs.title: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)
docs.text:
DeepSeek's alternative to GQA: keys and values are compressed into a small latent vector per token, which is what the KV cache stores; they are expanded again when attention runs (DeepSeek-V2, V3, R1).

Why it matters: Cuts the KV cache far more than GQA with no quality loss, which is how DeepSeek serves long contexts cheaply.

Index aliases: MLA

docs.title: Causal (masked) attention
docs.text:
Masking so a token can only attend to earlier tokens.

Why it matters: Stops the model from cheating by looking at the answer during training, and is what makes it generate left to right.

Index aliases: Causal mask, Masked attention

docs.title: Attention mask
docs.text:
The tensor that marks which positions may attend to which (causal mask, padding mask).

Why it matters: The practical implementation of "no peeking ahead" and "ignore padding".

docs.title: Quadratic cost of attention (O(n²))
docs.text:
Every token compares itself with every other, so compute and memory grow with the square of the sequence length.

Why it matters: Why long context is expensive and why FlashAttention, sliding windows and state-space models exist.

Index aliases: O(n²), O(n²) attention

docs.title: Sliding-window attention / attention sinks
docs.text:
Limiting each token to attend only to the last N tokens (sliding window), optionally keeping a few initial tokens always visible (attention sinks).

Why it matters: Makes very long inputs affordable at some cost in long-range recall; used in the original Mistral 7B and, mixed with global layers, in Gemma 2/3 and gpt-oss.

Index aliases: SWA, Attention sinks

docs.title: Cross-attention
docs.text:
The decoder attending to the encoder's outputs, in encoder-decoder models.

Why it matters: How a translator model reads the source sentence while writing the target one.

docs.title: Decoder-only model
docs.text:
Also known as: GPT, Llama, Claude, Gemini, Mistral

A Transformer with causal self-attention only, trained to predict the next token. The dominant LLM design.

Why it matters: Simplest design that scales; one model does understanding and generation. Almost every chat model is this.

docs.title: Encoder-only model
docs.text:
Also known as: BERT, RoBERTa

A bidirectional Transformer good at understanding, classification and embeddings, but not at generating text.

Why it matters: Still the usual choice for cheap classification and small, fast embedding models, because it reads both directions at once; many top-scoring embedding models are now built on decoder-only LLMs.

docs.title: Encoder-decoder model
docs.text:
Also known as: T5, BART, original Transformer

An encoder reads the input, a decoder writes the output.

Why it matters: Natural for translation and summarisation; largely displaced by decoder-only models that do everything.

Index aliases: T5 / BART

docs.title: Positional encoding / embedding
docs.text:
How the model knows token order, since attention by itself is order-blind. Sinusoidal in 2017, learned in GPT-2.

Why it matters: Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical to the model.

Index aliases: Positional embedding

docs.title: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE)
docs.text:
Today's standard positional scheme: encodes position by rotating the Q and K vectors so attention depends on relative distance.

Why it matters: Does not extrapolate well on its own, but can be cheaply stretched to longer contexts (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN), which is what makes 128k-token contexts practical.

Index aliases: RoPE

docs.title: ALiBi
docs.text:
Also known as: Attention with Linear Biases

A positional scheme with no position embeddings at all: a penalty proportional to the query–key distance is subtracted from each attention score, with a different slope per head (used by MPT and BLOOM).

Why it matters: Trains on short sequences and extrapolates to longer ones; the main rival to RoPE before RoPE won.

Index aliases: ALiBi (positional biases)

docs.title: Hidden state
docs.text:
The vector representing a token at a given layer; the residual stream's value at that point.

Why it matters: What gets passed from block to block, and what the LM head reads at the end. "Hidden size" = its length.

docs.title: Transformer block / layer
docs.text:
One unit of [attention → add & norm → feed-forward → add & norm]. Models stack 32 to 100+ of them.

Why it matters: The repeating unit; a model is this block copied N times with different weights. See Map 5.

docs.title: Feed-forward in a block
docs.text:
Also known as: MLP, SwiGLU

The per-token two-layer network after attention; it holds most of the parameters. SwiGLU is the gated variant most modern models use.

Why it matters: Attention moves information between tokens; the FFN processes it. Facts the model "knows" are mostly stored here.

docs.title: Residual stream
docs.text:
The running vector per token that every block adds its contribution to.

Why it matters: Each block reads from and writes to it, so information from early layers survives to the end.

docs.title: Attention Residuals (AttnRes)
docs.text:
A 2026 variant of the residual stream (Moonshot AI): instead of adding every earlier layer's output with a fixed weight of 1, each layer attends over earlier outputs with learned, softmax-normalised weights.

Why it matters: Small but consistent gains for ~4% extra training cost; a sign that even the residual stream is still being redesigned.

Index aliases: AttnRes

docs.title: Pre-norm vs post-norm
docs.text:
Whether normalization happens before or after each sub-layer. Pre-norm with RMSNorm is the modern choice.

Why it matters: Pre-norm trains more stably at scale, which is why GPT-2 onward switched to it.

Index aliases: Pre-norm

docs.title: QK-Norm
docs.text:
Also known as: query-key normalization

Normalize the query and key vectors (RMSNorm or LayerNorm) before computing attention scores (Gemma 3, OLMo 2, Qwen3).

Why it matters: Stops attention logits from blowing up, which removes a common cause of loss spikes and allows higher learning rates.

Index aliases: QKNorm

docs.title: d_model, n_heads, n_layers (hidden size)
docs.text:
The main shape hyperparameters of a Transformer: vector width per token, number of attention heads, number of stacked blocks.

Why it matters: Three numbers that describe a model's shape; parameter count follows from them (Map 5).

Index aliases: Hidden size

docs.title: Language-model head
docs.text:
Also known as: LM head, unembedding

The final linear layer mapping each token's hidden state to logits over the vocabulary.

Why it matters: Turns the model's internal vector into "a score for every possible next token".

docs.title: Weight tying
docs.text:
Reusing the token-embedding matrix as the LM head.

Why it matters: Saves a large chunk of parameters in small models (a third of GPT-2's).

docs.title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
docs.text:
Replaces each feed-forward layer with several experts and a router that activates only a few per token (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-MoE).

Why it matters: Huge knowledge capacity with the compute cost of a much smaller model: a 235B model that runs like a 22B one.

Index aliases: MoE

docs.title: Dense vs sparse model
docs.text:
A dense model uses all parameters for every token; a sparse (MoE) model uses a subset.

Why it matters: Explains names like "235B-A22B": 235B parameters total, 22B active per token.

Index aliases: Sparse model, Dense model

docs.title: FlashAttention
docs.text:
An exact but much faster, memory-efficient GPU implementation of attention.

Why it matters: Same maths, 2–4× faster and far less memory, by being clever about GPU memory traffic. An engineering trick, not a new architecture.

docs.title: State-space models / hybrids
docs.text:
Also known as: Mamba, SSM

Alternative sequence layers whose cost grows linearly with sequence length. Often mixed with attention layers.

Why it matters: A bet on cheaper long context; hybrids keep a few attention layers for precise recall.

docs.title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
docs.text:
A Transformer applied to image patches as if they were tokens.

Why it matters: Showed the same architecture works for images, which is what makes multimodal models possible.

Index aliases: ViT

docs.title: 7. Pre-training
docs.text:
Stage 3: the expensive phase that produces a base model

Weeks on thousands of GPUs, predicting the next token over trillions of tokens. Done by labs; the output is a base model that completes text but does not yet follow instructions.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Pre-training ★
docs.text:
The first and most expensive phase: train the randomly-initialised model on a massive corpus by predicting the next token.

Why it matters: Where the model learns language, facts and reasoning. Everything after only shapes how that knowledge is used.

docs.title: Next-token prediction ★
docs.text:
Also known as: causal language modelling, CLM

The pre-training objective: given the tokens so far, output a probability distribution over the next one.

Why it matters: A deceptively simple task: predicting the next word well enough requires understanding grammar, facts and logic.

Index aliases: Causal language modelling (CLM)

docs.title: Teacher forcing
docs.text:
During training the model sees the true previous tokens as input, not its own guesses, so all positions train in one parallel pass.

Why it matters: Why training is fast (whole sequence at once) while generation is slow (one token at a time).

docs.title: Masked language modelling (MLM)
docs.text:
The BERT-style objective: hide random tokens and predict them from both sides.

Why it matters: Produces excellent understanding models (and embeddings) but not text generators.

Index aliases: MLM, MLM (masked language modelling)

docs.title: Base model ★
docs.text:
The raw pre-trained model: continues text well, does not yet follow instructions or chat.

Why it matters: Ask it a question and it may continue with more questions. Post-training turns it into an assistant.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
A saved snapshot of the weights (and optimizer state) during or after training.

Why it matters: Lets a run resume after a crash and lets researchers compare the model at different points.

docs.title: Perplexity
docs.text:
The standard measure of how well a language model predicts text: exp(loss). Lower is better.

Why it matters: A perplexity of 10 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as choosing among 10 equally likely tokens.

Index aliases: PPL

docs.title: Loss curve / validation loss
docs.text:
Training loss over steps, alongside loss on held-out data. Validation loss rising while training loss falls means overfitting.

Why it matters: The main thing engineers watch during a run; a smooth downward curve means learning is working.

Index aliases: Validation loss

docs.title: Loss spikes / divergence
docs.text:
Sudden jumps in the loss during a long run: a bad batch, too high a learning rate or numerical trouble.

Why it matters: The nightmare of large training runs; gradient clipping, lower learning rates and restarting from a checkpoint are the usual fixes.

Index aliases: Loss spike

docs.title: Learning-rate schedule
docs.text:
Also known as: warmup, cosine decay, WSD

Ramp the learning rate up at the start, hold, then decay it toward the end.

Why it matters: Warmup prevents early blow-ups; decay lets the model settle into a good minimum. Standard practice for every LLM run.

Index aliases: Warmup / cosine decay

docs.title: Gradient clipping
docs.text:
Cap the gradient norm so one bad batch cannot blow up training.

Why it matters: A safety valve against exploding gradients and loss spikes.

docs.title: Gradient accumulation
docs.text:
Sum gradients over several mini-batches before updating.

Why it matters: Simulates a big batch on a small GPU, so you can train with less memory.

docs.title: Curriculum learning
docs.text:
Ordering training data from easy to hard, or changing the data mix over the course of training.

Why it matters: Can make training faster and the final model better than feeding everything in random order.

docs.title: Mixed precision
docs.text:
Also known as: FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8

Using lower-precision numbers for speed and memory while keeping a master copy of the weights in FP32. BF16 is the norm; FP8 is arriving.

Why it matters: Roughly doubles throughput and halves activation memory versus FP32, with no loss in quality when done right; weight and optimizer memory stay similar because the FP32 master copy remains.

Index aliases: BF16 / FP16 / FP8

docs.title: FLOPs / compute budget
docs.text:
The total floating-point operations a training run uses, roughly 6 × parameters × tokens.

Why it matters: Compute is the currency labs plan in; "10²⁵ FLOPs" is how regulators and papers describe a model's size of effort.

docs.title: Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU)
docs.text:
What fraction of the GPUs' theoretical peak compute the training run actually achieves (typically 30–50%).

Why it matters: The efficiency score of a training run; low MFU means expensive GPUs sitting idle waiting for data or communication.

Index aliases: MFU

docs.title: Scaling laws
docs.text:
The empirical finding that loss improves smoothly and predictably as you scale parameters, data and compute together.

Why it matters: Why labs bet billions: you can predict how much better a 10× bigger model will be before training it.

docs.title: Chinchilla-optimal
docs.text:
The 2022 rule of thumb of about 20 training tokens per parameter for a given training budget. Modern models are deliberately over-trained far beyond it.

Why it matters: Why an 8B model trained on 15T tokens beats older 70B models: small models are cheaper to serve, so extra training pays off.

Index aliases: Chinchilla, Compute-optimal, Over-training

docs.title: Emergent abilities
docs.text:
Capabilities that appear only once models pass a certain scale (a contested idea).

Why it matters: The argument for scaling: arithmetic or multi-step reasoning seemed to switch on at size.

docs.title: Data / tensor / pipeline parallelism
docs.text:
Three ways to split training across GPUs: by data batches, by slicing layers across devices, or by giving different layers to different devices.

Why it matters: How a model too big for one GPU is trained on thousands at once.

Index aliases: Tensor parallelism, Pipeline parallelism, Data parallelism

docs.title: FSDP / ZeRO
docs.text:
Also known as: Fully Sharded Data Parallel

Techniques that shard the weights, gradients and optimizer state across GPUs.

Why it matters: Lets models far bigger than one GPU's memory train without complex manual splitting.

Index aliases: FSDP, ZeRO (DeepSpeed)

docs.title: Continued pre-training
docs.text:
Keep pre-training a base model on new domain data (medical, legal, a new language, your company's docs) before any instruction tuning.

Why it matters: The way to add deep domain knowledge or a new language; much cheaper than training from scratch, much heavier than fine-tuning.

docs.title: Mid-training / annealing
docs.text:
The final pre-training phase on a higher-quality data mix with a decaying learning rate.

Why it matters: Increasingly where labs tune knowledge quality and inject maths, code and long-context ability.

Index aliases: Annealing, Mid-training

docs.title: 8. Post-training & alignment
docs.text:
Stage 4: turning a base model into an assistant

Done by the lab after pre-training, historically at a small fraction of the cost (though for the newest reasoning models the RL phase is growing toward pre-training scale). Supervised examples teach the format, then reinforcement learning shapes behaviour. Confusingly, people also call this "fine-tuning" or "alignment".

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Post-training
docs.text:
Everything the lab does after pre-training to make the model useful and safe: SFT, preference optimization, reinforcement learning.

Why it matters: Turns a text-completer into an assistant. Most of what you feel as the model's "personality" was shaped here.

docs.title: Fine-tuning (general meaning)
docs.text:
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller, targeted dataset. Labs do it (post-training) and you can do it (section 9).

Why it matters: Same mechanics as pre-training, far less data. The word means two different stages depending on who is speaking.

docs.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning ★
docs.text:
Also known as: SFT, instruction tuning

Train on curated prompt → ideal-answer pairs so the model learns to follow instructions and hold a conversation.

Why it matters: Teaches the model the format of being helpful: answer the question, use the chat template, stop when done.

docs.title: Instruct / chat model
docs.text:
The model after post-training. What you actually talk to.

Why it matters: The "-Instruct" or "-Chat" suffix on a model name means it has been through this stage.

Index aliases: Chat model, Instruct model

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
Making the model's behaviour match human intentions and values; often summarised as helpful, harmless and honest (HHH).

Why it matters: Both a goal (the model behaves as intended) and the name of the RLHF / safety part of post-training.

Index aliases: HHH (helpful, harmless, honest)

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ★
docs.text:
Humans rank model outputs → train a reward model on those rankings → use RL (PPO) to push the model toward higher-reward answers.

Why it matters: Makes answers more helpful and polite than SFT alone, because it optimises for what people actually prefer. The technique behind ChatGPT.

Index aliases: RLHF

docs.title: Reward model (RM)
docs.text:
A model trained to score how good an answer is, standing in for human judgement during reinforcement learning.

Why it matters: Lets RL run millions of times without a human in the loop: the reward model is the automated judge.

Index aliases: RM, Reward model (RM)

docs.title: Preference data
docs.text:
Also known as: pairwise comparisons

"Answer A is better than answer B" data used to train reward models or directly in DPO.

Why it matters: Cheaper to collect than ideal answers: comparing two outputs is easier than writing a perfect one.

docs.title: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
docs.text:
The RL algorithm classically used in RLHF. Updates the policy in small clipped steps.

Why it matters: Keeps RL training stable: small steps mean the model cannot suddenly wander into nonsense.

Index aliases: PPO

docs.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
docs.text:
Trains directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss, skipping the reward model and the RL loop.

Why it matters: Gets most of RLHF's benefit with a fraction of the complexity, which is why open-model teams love it.

Index aliases: DPO

docs.title: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
docs.text:
A PPO variant that samples a group of answers to the same prompt and scores each relative to the group, with no separate value model. Used by DeepSeek-R1.

Why it matters: Cheaper and simpler than PPO, and it turned out to be the recipe for training reasoning models.

Index aliases: GRPO, DeepSeek-R1

docs.title: Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO)
docs.text:
The Qwen team's 2025 successor to GRPO: the importance ratio and clipping are computed per whole sequence instead of per token. Used to train the Qwen3 Instruct, Coder and Thinking models.

Why it matters: More stable RL training, especially for Mixture-of-Experts models, where token-level GRPO tends to collapse.

Index aliases: GSPO

docs.title: On-policy vs off-policy
docs.text:
On-policy methods (PPO, GRPO) learn from answers the current model just generated; off-policy methods (DPO on a fixed dataset) learn from stored data.

Why it matters: On-policy is more expensive but keeps improving the model on its own mistakes; off-policy is cheap but can go stale.

docs.title: RLAIF / Constitutional AI
docs.text:
Use an AI, guided by a written set of principles (a constitution), to produce the feedback instead of, or alongside, humans. Anthropic's approach.

Why it matters: Scales feedback far beyond what human raters can produce, and makes the rules explicit and inspectable.

Index aliases: Constitutional AI, RLAIF

docs.title: RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)
docs.text:
Reinforcement learning where the reward is an automatic check: did the maths answer match, did the unit tests pass.

Why it matters: No reward model to fool: when the answer is checkable, RL can push the model far beyond human demonstrations. The key ingredient of reasoning models.

Index aliases: RLVR

docs.title: Outcome vs process reward model
docs.text:
Also known as: ORM, PRM

An ORM scores only the final answer; a PRM scores each step of the reasoning.

Why it matters: Step-level rewards give the model more precise feedback on where it went wrong, at a higher labelling cost.

Index aliases: PRM / ORM

docs.title: Reasoning / thinking model
docs.text:
A model post-trained to produce a long chain of thought before answering (OpenAI o-series, DeepSeek-R1, Claude extended thinking, Gemini thinking).

Why it matters: Much more accurate on maths, code and multi-step problems, in exchange for more tokens and latency.

Index aliases: o1 / o3, Extended thinking

docs.title: Thinking budget / reasoning tokens
docs.text:
The number of tokens a reasoning model may spend thinking before it answers; often a setting you control. Reasoning tokens are usually billed as output.

Why it matters: Lets you trade cost and speed for accuracy per request.

Index aliases: Reasoning tokens

docs.title: Test-time compute / inference-time scaling
docs.text:
Spending more compute at answer time (longer thinking, multiple samples, search) to get better answers, instead of only training a bigger model.

Why it matters: The second scaling axis: the same model gets smarter if you let it think longer.

Index aliases: Inference-time scaling

docs.title: Agentic / multi-turn RL
docs.text:
Reinforcement learning on whole tasks that involve many steps and tool calls, not single answers.

Why it matters: How models are trained to be good at long coding sessions and browsing, not only at one-shot replies.

docs.title: KL penalty / reference model
docs.text:
A term in the RL objective keeping the trained model close to the SFT model.

Why it matters: Stops the model from drifting into gibberish that happens to score well with the reward model.

Index aliases: Reference model, KL divergence

docs.title: Reward hacking
docs.text:
The model finding ways to get high reward without actually being good: verbosity, confident tone, telling the grader what it wants.

Why it matters: Why RL needs careful rewards: optimise a flawed score and you get a flawed model.

docs.title: Sycophancy
docs.text:
The tendency to agree with the user over telling the truth.

Why it matters: A known side effect of optimising for human approval; worth remembering when a model agrees with you too easily.

docs.title: Rejection sampling / Best-of-N
docs.text:
Generate N answers, keep the best according to a judge or reward model, then train on those.

Why it matters: A simple, strong post-training method: let the model teach itself from its own best attempts.

Index aliases: Best-of-N

docs.title: Distillation
docs.text:
Train a smaller student model to imitate a bigger teacher's outputs.

Why it matters: How small, cheap models get surprisingly capable: they copy the behaviour of a frontier model.

docs.title: Model merging
docs.text:
Averaging or combining the weights of several fine-tuned models into one.

Why it matters: Combines skills from different fine-tunes without retraining; cheap and oddly effective.

docs.title: Safety training / refusals
docs.text:
Post-training the model to decline harmful requests and handle sensitive topics carefully.

Why it matters: Why a model says no to some requests; the behaviour is learned here, not hard-coded.

docs.title: 9. Adapting a model to your task
docs.text:
Stage 5: your own fine-tuning on an open-weight or API model

This is where a company or an individual steps in. Usually hours on one GPU with a few thousand examples. Try prompting and RAG first (Map 7); fine-tune for style, format, latency or truly niche tasks.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Fine-tuning (your version) ★
docs.text:
Taking an open-weight model (or an API fine-tuning endpoint) and training it further on your own examples to change its style, format or domain behaviour.

Why it matters: Makes a general model behave your way: consistent format, your tone, your domain's conventions, often with a smaller and cheaper model.

docs.title: Full fine-tuning
docs.text:
Update all the weights.

Why it matters: Highest quality ceiling but needs the most GPU memory and risks forgetting general skills.

docs.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
docs.text:
A family of methods that freeze the model and train only a small set of extra parameters.

Why it matters: Fine-tune a big model on a single GPU and store the result as a tiny file.

Index aliases: PEFT

docs.title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ★
docs.text:
The most popular PEFT method: learn small low-rank matrices that are added to the attention and feed-forward weights.

Why it matters: Trains ~1% of the parameters for most of the benefit; the adapter is a small file (tens to a couple of hundred MB) you can swap in and out.

Index aliases: LoRA

docs.title: QLoRA
docs.text:
LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base model.

Why it matters: Lets you fine-tune a 65–70B model on a single 48 GB GPU, or a 7–13B model on a consumer card.

Index aliases: QLoRA (4-bit LoRA)

docs.title: Adapters, prompt tuning, prefix tuning
docs.text:
Other PEFT flavours: small bottleneck layers inserted in the network, or learned soft-prompt vectors prepended to the input.

Why it matters: Same goal as LoRA (cheap adaptation), different mechanics; LoRA won on simplicity.

Index aliases: Prefix tuning / prompt tuning

docs.title: Rank (r) and alpha
docs.text:
LoRA hyperparameters controlling adapter size and how strongly it is scaled.

Why it matters: Higher rank = more capacity and memory; typical values are 8–64.

Index aliases: Rank / alpha (LoRA)

docs.title: Merging an adapter
docs.text:
Adding the trained LoRA matrices into the base weights to produce a single standalone model.

Why it matters: Removes the small inference overhead of a separate adapter and gives you one file to deploy.

Index aliases: Adapter (LoRA)

docs.title: Task / classification head
docs.text:
A small new output layer placed on top of the model for a specific task (e.g. spam / not spam), replacing the LM head. (Raschka chapter 6.)

Why it matters: The simplest fine-tune: reuse everything the model knows, train only the last layer for your labels.

Index aliases: Classification head

docs.title: Catastrophic forgetting
docs.text:
Fine-tuning on a narrow dataset erodes the general abilities the model had before.

Why it matters: Why you keep the learning rate low, mix in general data, and prefer LoRA: to add a skill without losing the others.

docs.title: Domain adaptation
docs.text:
Specialising a general model to a field: legal, medical, your codebase, your product's tone.

Why it matters: Makes the model fluent in your world's vocabulary and conventions.

docs.title: Instruction dataset
docs.text:
The prompt → completion pairs you fine-tune on. Quality matters more than quantity; hundreds to a few thousand good examples often suffice.

Why it matters: Your main lever: the model will copy whatever these examples do, including their mistakes.

docs.title: Dataset formats
docs.text:
Also known as: Alpaca, ShareGPT, messages / JSONL

Standard JSON layouts for instruction data: Alpaca (instruction / input / output), ShareGPT (conversations), or OpenAI-style messages lists.

Why it matters: The format most fine-tuning tools expect; converting your data into one of these is step one.

Index aliases: Alpaca / ShareGPT format

docs.title: Open weights vs open source
docs.text:
Open weights means you can download and fine-tune the parameters (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma). True open source also releases the data and training code (OLMo).

Why it matters: Open weights are what let you fine-tune and self-host; "open source" is usually a looser claim.

Index aliases: Qwen, Open weights, Open source (models)

docs.title: API fine-tuning
docs.text:
Fine-tuning a closed model through the provider's API: you upload examples, they train and host the result.

Why it matters: Fine-tuning without GPUs or ops; the trade-off is lock-in and less control.

docs.title: Hugging Face PEFT / TRL / Unsloth / Axolotl
docs.text:
The standard libraries and tools for running LoRA, SFT and DPO on open models.

Why it matters: The tools most fine-tuning tutorials use; Unsloth is the fast, memory-light one for single GPUs.

Index aliases: Unsloth / Axolotl, TRL

docs.title: Evaluation set
docs.text:
A held-out slice of your own examples used to check the fine-tune actually improved things.

Why it matters: The only way to know your fine-tune helped and did not just overfit your examples.

docs.title: 10. Inference & serving
docs.text:
Stage 6: running the model to produce tokens, fast and cheaply

No weights change here. Everything is about choosing the next token well, and about memory, latency and cost. Map 4 shows the whole request path.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Inference ★
docs.text:
Using a trained model to produce output. No weights change.

Why it matters: What every API call and chat message is. The cost and speed of AI products are decided here.

docs.title: Autoregressive generation
docs.text:
Produce one token, append it to the input, run again, until a stop token or the max length is reached.

Why it matters: Why text appears word by word, and why long answers take proportionally longer.

docs.title: Prefill vs decode
docs.text:
Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass (compute-bound). Decode produces tokens one at a time (memory-bound).

Why it matters: Explains the two numbers you feel: a pause before the first token (prefill), then a steady stream (decode).

Index aliases: Prefill, Decode

docs.title: KV cache
docs.text:
Storing the keys and values of all previous tokens so each new token does not recompute them.

Why it matters: Makes generation many times faster; its memory size is the main limit on long contexts and many parallel users.

docs.title: Decoding strategy
docs.text:
How the next token is chosen from the probability distribution the model outputs.

Why it matters: The same model can sound careful or creative depending only on this choice.

docs.title: Greedy decoding
docs.text:
Always pick the most probable token.

Why it matters: Deterministic and fast, but tends to repeat itself and miss better overall sentences.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
Pick the next token randomly according to the model's probabilities.

Why it matters: Gives variety and more natural text; the reason the same prompt gives different answers.

docs.title: Temperature ★
docs.text:
Scales the logits before softmax. Low values make output focused and near-deterministic, high values make it diverse and random. 0 is effectively greedy.

Why it matters: Your main creativity knob: low for code and facts, higher for brainstorming.

docs.title: Top-k / Top-p (nucleus) sampling
docs.text:
Only sample from the k most likely tokens, or from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.

Why it matters: Cuts off the long tail of nonsense tokens so sampling stays creative but coherent.

Index aliases: Nucleus sampling, Top-p, Top-k

docs.title: Beam search
docs.text:
Keep several candidate sequences and expand the best ones.

Why it matters: Finds higher-probability whole sentences; common in translation, rarely used in chat because it sounds bland.

docs.title: Repetition / frequency penalty
docs.text:
Lower the probability of tokens that have already appeared.

Why it matters: Stops the model from looping on the same phrase.

Index aliases: Frequency penalty

docs.title: Constrained / grammar-based decoding
docs.text:
Restricting sampling so the output must follow a grammar or JSON schema.

Why it matters: Guarantees valid JSON or a fixed set of choices, rather than hoping the model complies.

Index aliases: Grammar-constrained decoding

docs.title: Logprobs
docs.text:
The log-probabilities of generated tokens, which APIs can expose.

Why it matters: A cheap confidence signal: low probability on a key token is a hint the model is guessing.

docs.title: Max tokens / stop sequences
docs.text:
The limit on output length, and strings that end generation early.

Why it matters: Controls cost and prevents run-on answers.

Index aliases: Stop sequence, Max tokens

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Sending tokens to the client as they are generated.

Why it matters: Makes a 10-second answer feel instant because the user starts reading immediately.

docs.title: Latency: TTFT, TPOT, tokens/sec
docs.text:
Also known as: time to first token, time per output token

Time to first token measures prefill. Time per output token (the gap between tokens, also called inter-token latency) measures decode; tokens per second is its inverse.

Why it matters: The numbers users feel: optimise TTFT for chat, TPOT for long outputs.

Index aliases: TPOT, Inter-token latency, TTFT, Tokens per second

docs.title: Throughput / batching / continuous batching
docs.text:
Serving many requests at once by batching their decode steps. Continuous batching slots new requests in mid-stream.

Why it matters: Serves many more users per GPU, which is what makes API prices possible.

Index aliases: Continuous batching

docs.title: PagedAttention / vLLM
docs.text:
Managing the KV cache like virtual-memory pages so GPU memory is not wasted. vLLM is the open-source engine that popularised it.

Why it matters: Fits more simultaneous requests in the same GPU memory, roughly 2–4× the throughput.

Index aliases: vLLM, PagedAttention

docs.title: Quantization
docs.text:
Also known as: INT8, INT4, FP8

Storing weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits.

Why it matters: Cuts memory 2–4× and speeds up inference, at a small quality cost; how a 70B model fits on one GPU or a laptop.

Index aliases: INT8 / INT4

docs.title: GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ
docs.text:
Common quantized formats and methods. GGUF is the format llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio use.

Why it matters: When a download page lists "Q4_K_M", it is a 4-bit GGUF file ready for local use.

Index aliases: GGUF, GPTQ / AWQ

docs.title: Speculative decoding
docs.text:
A small draft model proposes several tokens, the big model verifies them in one pass.

Why it matters: Same output as the big model, noticeably faster, because verifying is cheaper than generating.

docs.title: Serving engines
docs.text:
Also known as: vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, TGI, llama.cpp, Ollama

Software that loads weights and serves requests efficiently: the first four for servers, the last two for laptops.

Why it matters: The difference between a demo and a production service; they handle batching, caching and memory for you.

docs.title: Prompt caching
docs.text:
Reusing the KV cache for a repeated prefix (a long system prompt, a set of documents) across requests.

Why it matters: Cuts cost and latency sharply when many requests share the same long beginning.

docs.title: Semantic caching
docs.text:
Caching whole answers keyed by the meaning of the question, so a similar question returns the stored answer without calling the model.

Why it matters: Avoids paying for the same answer twice when users ask the same thing in different words.

docs.title: Model routing / cascades
docs.text:
Sending each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it, escalating to a bigger one only when needed.

Why it matters: Big cost savings with little quality loss, because most requests are easy.

Index aliases: Cascades

docs.title: Batch API, rate limits
docs.text:
Providers offer discounted non-urgent batch processing, and cap how many requests and tokens you can send per minute.

Why it matters: Shapes system design: batch what can wait, queue and retry for the rest.

Index aliases: Rate limits

docs.title: Long context / context extension
docs.text:
