Running models beyond their trained length with positional scaling tricks (RoPE scaling, YaRN) and better attention kernels.

Why it matters: How 4k-context models became 128k; recall at the far end of the window is still weaker.

Index aliases: YaRN / RoPE scaling

docs.title: On-device / edge inference
docs.text:
Running small quantized models on phones and laptops with no server.

Why it matters: Private, offline and free per use; the trade-off is a much smaller model.

Index aliases: Edge inference

docs.title: Model size vs memory
docs.text:
Rule of thumb: parameters × bytes per weight. A 7B model is about 14 GB in 16-bit and about 4 GB at 4-bit, plus the KV cache.

Why it matters: Quick way to know whether a model fits your GPU or laptop before downloading it.

docs.title: 11. Building applications
docs.text:
Stage 7: prompting, retrieval, tools and agents around a frozen model

Where most engineers spend their time. The model is a component; the system around it (Map 6) decides whether the product works.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text:
The text you send to the model: instructions, context, question.

Why it matters: The model's entire view of your task; everything it does not say, the model does not know.

docs.title: System prompt ★
docs.text:
Instructions set by the developer that frame the whole conversation: persona, rules, available tools, output format.

Why it matters: Your main control surface as an engineer; most product behaviour is written here, not trained.

docs.title: Prompt engineering
docs.text:
Crafting prompts to get reliable results: clear instructions, examples, explicit output format, role, constraints. Prompts are versioned and tested like code.

Why it matters: The cheapest and fastest way to improve a model's output; always the first thing to try.

Index aliases: Prompt template

docs.title: Zero-shot / few-shot
docs.text:
Asking with no examples versus including a few worked examples in the prompt.

Why it matters: A couple of examples in the prompt often beat pages of instructions.

Index aliases: Few-shot, Zero-shot

docs.title: In-context learning (ICL)
docs.text:
The model's ability to pick up a task from examples in the prompt without any weight updates.

Why it matters: Why few-shot works: the model adapts on the fly, no training needed.

Index aliases: ICL

docs.title: Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
docs.text:
Asking the model to reason step by step before answering.

Why it matters: Noticeably more accurate on reasoning tasks because the model gets to "use scratch paper"; reasoning models bake this in.

Index aliases: CoT

docs.title: Self-consistency / majority voting
docs.text:
Sample several answers and take the most common one.

Why it matters: A simple way to buy accuracy with more compute; a form of test-time scaling you can do from the outside.

Index aliases: Majority voting

docs.title: Tree of Thoughts / search
docs.text:
Explore several reasoning paths, evaluate them, and expand the promising ones, instead of one linear chain.

Why it matters: Better on hard planning problems; the application-level cousin of MCTS.

Index aliases: Tree of Thoughts

docs.title: Structured outputs / JSON mode
docs.text:
Forcing the model to answer in a machine-readable format, often validated against a schema.

Why it matters: Makes model output safe to parse in code, which any real integration needs.

Index aliases: JSON mode

docs.title: Function calling / tool use
docs.text:
The model emits a structured request (call get_weather with city = Kraków), your code runs it and returns the result for the model to continue.

Why it matters: Lets the model act on the world and fetch live data instead of guessing from memory.

Index aliases: Tool use, Function calling

docs.title: Agent ★
docs.text:
An LLM in a loop: observe → decide → act with tools → observe the result, until the task is done.

Why it matters: Turns a chatbot into something that completes multi-step tasks: fixing a bug, booking a trip, researching a question.

docs.title: Workflows vs agents
docs.text:
A workflow is a fixed sequence of LLM calls you program; an agent decides its own next step at runtime.

Why it matters: Workflows are predictable and cheap; agents are flexible and harder to control. Use the simplest one that works.

docs.title: Agentic workflow, ReAct, planning
docs.text:
Patterns for structuring agents: interleaving reasoning and actions (ReAct), explicit plans, decomposition into sub-tasks, reflection.

Why it matters: Known recipes that make agents more reliable than a bare loop.

Index aliases: ReAct

docs.title: Multi-agent system
docs.text:
Several specialised agents (planner, coder, reviewer, researcher) coordinating on one task.

Why it matters: Splits a big job into roles with separate contexts; helps on long tasks, adds coordination overhead.

Index aliases: Multi-agent

docs.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
docs.text:
An open standard for connecting models to tools and data sources through a common server interface, so any MCP client can use any MCP server.

Why it matters: Write a tool once, use it from every assistant: the "USB-C of AI tools". Your Spring AI servers speak this.

Index aliases: MCP

docs.title: Agent-to-Agent protocol (A2A)
docs.text:
A standard for agents from different vendors to discover each other and exchange tasks.

Why it matters: MCP connects an agent to tools; A2A connects agents to agents.

Index aliases: A2A

docs.title: Computer-use / browser agents
docs.text:
Agents that operate a screen, browser or terminal through screenshots, clicks and keystrokes.

Why it matters: Lets a model use software that has no API, which is most software.

Index aliases: Computer use, Browser agent

docs.title: Agentic coding
docs.text:
Also known as: Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot agent mode

Coding assistants that read a repository, edit files, run tests and iterate on their own. "Vibe coding" is building by describing what you want and accepting the result.

Why it matters: The most widely adopted agent use case; changes how software gets written.

Index aliases: Vibe coding, Cursor / Copilot

docs.title: Sandboxing
docs.text:
Running an agent's code and tool calls in an isolated environment with limited permissions.

Why it matters: Contains the damage when an agent makes a mistake or is tricked by prompt injection.

Index aliases: Sandbox

docs.title: Human-in-the-loop (HITL)
docs.text:
Requiring a person to approve certain steps (sending the email, deleting the file, paying).

Why it matters: The standard safety net for agents taking real actions.

Index aliases: HITL

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ★
docs.text:
Fetch relevant documents (search or vector database) and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data.

Why it matters: Gives the model knowledge it was never trained on, kept up to date, with sources, without any training.

Index aliases: RAG, Agentic RAG

docs.title: Text embeddings
docs.text:
Vectors representing the meaning of a text chunk; similar texts land near each other. Produced by a separate embedding model.

Why it matters: The basis of semantic search: find documents by meaning, not by matching keywords.

Index aliases: Embedding model

docs.title: Vector database
docs.text:
Also known as: pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant; FAISS is the underlying index library

A store that indexes embeddings for fast nearest-neighbour search.

Why it matters: Finds the 10 most relevant chunks out of millions in milliseconds.

Index aliases: Pinecone / Weaviate / Qdrant, FAISS

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
Splitting documents into pieces small enough to embed and retrieve.

Why it matters: Chunk size and overlap decide whether retrieval finds the right passage; one of the most-tuned RAG knobs.

docs.title: Semantic / hybrid search
docs.text:
Searching by embedding similarity; hybrid search combines it with classic keyword search (BM25).

Why it matters: Hybrid catches both "same meaning, different words" and exact identifiers like error codes.

Index aliases: BM25 / keyword search, Hybrid search

docs.title: Reranker
docs.text:
A second model that re-orders retrieved chunks by relevance before they go into the prompt.

Why it matters: Cheap accuracy boost for RAG: retrieve 50 loosely, keep the best 5 precisely.

docs.title: Grounding / citations
docs.text:
Tying answers to retrieved sources so claims can be checked.

Why it matters: Reduces hallucination and lets users verify; does not eliminate it.

Index aliases: Citations

docs.title: Context engineering
docs.text:
Managing everything in the context window (system prompt, retrieved docs, tool results, memory) so the model has what it needs and nothing more.

Why it matters: Too little context and the model guesses; too much and it gets lost and costs more. Good agents are mostly good context management.

docs.title: Memory (short- and long-term)
docs.text:
Conversation history inside the context window versus facts stored outside and retrieved later.

Why it matters: How an assistant remembers you across sessions: it is retrieval, not training.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
Input and output checks (classifiers, rules, schemas) placed around the model.

Why it matters: Catches bad inputs and bad outputs the model itself might let through.

Index aliases: Guardrail

docs.title: Prompt injection
docs.text:
An attack where untrusted content (a web page, an email, a document) contains instructions the model wrongly follows.

Why it matters: The top security risk for agents: anything the model reads can try to give it orders.

docs.title: LLM-as-a-judge
docs.text:
Using a strong model to grade another model's outputs at scale.

Why it matters: Makes evaluation cheap enough to run on every change, like unit tests for prompts.

Index aliases: LaaJ, Judge model

docs.title: Orchestration frameworks
docs.text:
Also known as: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Spring AI, Semantic Kernel, Agent SDKs

Libraries wiring prompts, tools, retrieval and agents together.

Why it matters: Save boilerplate; the concepts underneath are the ones in this section.

Index aliases: LangChain / LlamaIndex

docs.title: Observability / tracing
docs.text:
Also known as: LangSmith, Langfuse, OpenTelemetry

Logging prompts, tool calls, tokens, cost and latency per request.

Why it matters: You cannot improve an LLM app you cannot see; tracing shows why a given answer went wrong.

Index aliases: LangSmith / Langfuse

docs.title: Hallucination ★
docs.text:
Confident, fluent, wrong output.

Why it matters: The model is predicting plausible text, not checking facts. RAG, tools and grounding reduce it; nothing eliminates it.

docs.title: Token pricing
docs.text:
APIs bill per input token and per output token. Output tokens cost more; cached input tokens cost less.

Why it matters: Why prompt length, answer length and caching are the three cost levers.

docs.title: 12. Evaluation, safety & interpretability
docs.text:
Cross-cutting: measuring, attacking and understanding models at every stage

These terms show up at every stage: a loss curve during pre-training, red-teaming before release, an eval set for your own fine-tune.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: Evals / evaluation
docs.text:
Any systematic measurement of model quality: benchmarks, human ratings, your own test sets.

Why it matters: The only way to know whether a change helped; "it feels better" is not evidence.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
A fixed dataset plus a scoring rule for comparing models.

Why it matters: How leaderboards are made; useful, and easy to game.

docs.title: MMLU / MMLU-Pro
docs.text:
Multiple-choice knowledge questions across 57 subjects; MMLU-Pro is the harder successor with 10 answer options across 14 disciplines.

Why it matters: The classic general-knowledge score; now saturated for top models.

Index aliases: MMLU

docs.title: GSM8K, MATH, AIME
docs.text:
Maths benchmarks from grade-school word problems up to competition level.

Why it matters: Where reasoning models show the biggest jumps.

Index aliases: GSM8K, AIME

docs.title: HumanEval, SWE-bench
docs.text:
Code benchmarks: generating functions from docstrings, and fixing real GitHub issues end to end.

Why it matters: SWE-bench (Verified) is the number to watch for coding agents.

Index aliases: SWE-bench, HumanEval

docs.title: GPQA
docs.text:
Graduate-level science questions designed to be Google-proof.

Why it matters: Tests deep expertise rather than memorised trivia.

docs.title: ARC-AGI, Humanity's Last Exam
docs.text:
Benchmarks designed to stay hard: abstract visual puzzles (ARC-AGI) and expert questions across every field (HLE).

Why it matters: The current frontier benchmarks; when older ones saturate, these are what headlines quote.

Index aliases: HLE (Humanity's Last Exam), ARC-AGI

docs.title: Agentic benchmarks
docs.text:
Also known as: SWE-bench Verified, τ-bench, Terminal-Bench

Benchmarks scoring a model on multi-step tasks with tools, not single answers.

Why it matters: Measure what matters for agents: finishing the job, not answering a question.

Index aliases: τ-bench / Terminal-Bench

docs.title: Needle in a haystack
docs.text:
Hide one fact in a very long document and check whether the model can retrieve it.

Why it matters: The standard test of whether a long context window really works.

Index aliases: NIAH

docs.title: pass@k
docs.text:
The chance that at least one of k generated attempts is correct.

Why it matters: Used for code and maths; pass@1 is what a user experiences, pass@10 shows the model's potential with search.

docs.title: Chatbot Arena / LMArena / Elo
docs.text:
Crowd-sourced blind comparisons of models, producing an Elo-style leaderboard.

Why it matters: The closest thing to "which model do people prefer".

Index aliases: LMArena / Chatbot Arena, Elo rating

docs.title: Data contamination
docs.text:
Benchmark questions leaking into training data, inflating scores.

Why it matters: Why benchmark numbers are treated with suspicion and why private test sets exist.

Index aliases: Contamination

docs.title: Factuality / hallucination rate
docs.text:
The fraction of generated claims that are unsupported or false.

Why it matters: The metric that matters most for RAG and research assistants.

Index aliases: Factuality

docs.title: Bias and fairness
docs.text:
Systematic differences in model behaviour across groups of people.

Why it matters: A legal and ethical requirement in hiring, lending and medicine.

docs.title: Robustness
docs.text:
Stability of answers under rephrasing, typos, noise and adversarial inputs.

Why it matters: A model that changes its answer over a comma is not production-ready.

docs.title: Explainability
docs.text:
Also known as: SHAP, LIME

Methods that attribute a classic-ML prediction to the features that drove it.

Why it matters: Required in regulated decisions; the classic-ML cousin of LLM interpretability.

Index aliases: SHAP / LIME, Explainability (SHAP, LIME)

docs.title: Red teaming
docs.text:
Deliberately attacking a model to find harmful or broken behaviour before release.

Why it matters: Finds failures before users (or attackers) do.

Index aliases: Red team

docs.title: Jailbreak
docs.text:
A prompt that tricks the model into ignoring its safety training.

Why it matters: Safety behaviour is learned, not enforced, so defences are layered.

Index aliases: Jailbreaking

docs.title: Over-refusal
docs.text:
A model declining harmless requests because they superficially resemble harmful ones.

Why it matters: The other side of safety training; labs tune to minimise both harm and over-refusal.

docs.title: AI safety / responsible scaling
docs.text:
Also known as: RSP, safety levels

The field concerned with preventing harm from AI systems, from today's misuse to risks at larger scale. Responsible-scaling policies tie capability thresholds to the safeguards required before release.

Why it matters: Where alignment, red teaming and safety levels come from; how labs commit to not shipping a model until matching safeguards exist.

Index aliases: Responsible Scaling Policy, ASL (AI Safety Level), AI safety

docs.title: Sandbagging / evaluation awareness
docs.text:
A model behaving differently when it suspects it is being tested, even hiding capabilities.

Why it matters: A newer safety concern: evals are only trustworthy if the model cannot tell it is being evaluated.

Index aliases: Evaluation awareness, Sandbagging

docs.title: Scalable oversight
docs.text:
Techniques for humans to supervise models on tasks they cannot fully judge themselves (debate, AI-assisted review).

Why it matters: The long-term question of alignment: how to check work better than yours.

docs.title: Interpretability / mechanistic interpretability
docs.text:
Studying what happens inside the network: which neurons, features and circuits do what.

Why it matters: Lets researchers see why a model answered as it did, instead of a black box.

Index aliases: Mechanistic interpretability

docs.title: Features, superposition, Sparse Autoencoders (SAE)
docs.text:
Features are the interpretable concepts a model represents; superposition is the finding that it packs more features than it has neurons; Sparse Autoencoders are the tool that unmixes activations into those features.

Why it matters: Found concrete concepts inside models (a "Golden Gate Bridge" feature); a path to steering and auditing.

Index aliases: SAE, Sparse Autoencoder (SAE), Superposition

docs.title: Model card / system card
docs.text:
Documentation of a model's training, capabilities, limits and safety testing.

Why it matters: Where to look before trusting a model.

Index aliases: System card

docs.title: 13. Infrastructure & ecosystem
docs.text:
Cross-cutting: the hardware and software everything runs on

Why NVIDIA, Hugging Face and PyTorch come up in every video.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
Also known as: NVIDIA H100 / B200, AMD MI300

The massively parallel processor that does nearly all training and inference.

Why it matters: Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplication, and GPUs do thousands of those in parallel; the reason AI progress tracks GPU supply.

Index aliases: H100 / B200, NVIDIA

docs.title: TPU
docs.text:
Google's custom accelerator, used for Gemini and available on Google Cloud.

Why it matters: The main non-NVIDIA option at frontier scale.

Index aliases: TPU (Google)

docs.title: Custom inference chips
docs.text:
Also known as: Groq LPU, Cerebras, Trainium, Inferentia

Accelerators designed specifically for running (or training) models, often with very high token speed.

Why it matters: Why some providers serve 500+ tokens per second. (NVIDIA licensed Groq's technology in late 2025.)

Index aliases: Groq / Cerebras

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
NVIDIA's GPU programming platform.

Why it matters: The software moat: most frameworks and kernels target CUDA first, which keeps the ecosystem NVIDIA-first.

docs.title: VRAM / HBM (GPU memory)
docs.text:
The GPU's memory. 80 GB on an H100, 24 GB on a consumer RTX 4090.

Why it matters: The hard limit on which models fit; most "can I run this?" questions are about VRAM.

Index aliases: VRAM, HBM

docs.title: Out of memory
docs.text:
Also known as: OOM, CUDA OOM

The error when a model, batch or KV cache does not fit in GPU memory.

Why it matters: The most common error in any training or serving tutorial; fixes are smaller batch, quantization, gradient accumulation or a bigger GPU.

Index aliases: OOM (out of memory)

docs.title: NVLink, InfiniBand, cluster
docs.text:
High-speed interconnects joining thousands of GPUs into one training machine.

Why it matters: Training a frontier model is as much a networking problem as a maths problem.

Index aliases: InfiniBand / NVLink

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text:
The dominant deep-learning framework, and what Raschka's book uses. JAX (Google) and TensorFlow are the alternatives.

Why it matters: Nearly every tutorial, paper and model release is in PyTorch; learn it first.

Index aliases: JAX / TensorFlow

docs.title: Hugging Face
docs.text:
Also known as: Transformers library, Hub

The de-facto library and repository for open models, datasets and tokenizers.

Why it matters: The GitHub of models: where you download weights and the library that loads them in three lines.

Index aliases: Hugging Face Hub

docs.title: Safetensors / weights file
docs.text:
The standard file format for storing model parameters safely (no arbitrary code on load).

Why it matters: The file you actually download; safe to open unlike the older pickle format.

Index aliases: Safetensors

docs.title: Parameter count
docs.text:
Also known as: 7B, 70B, 405B

Model size in billions of weights.

Why it matters: A quick proxy for capability, memory and cost; the first number anyone quotes about a model.

docs.title: Model API
docs.text:
Also known as: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Bedrock, Vertex

Hosted access to a model: you send tokens, you get tokens, you pay per token.

Why it matters: The way most products use frontier models: no GPUs, no ops, pay per use.

docs.title: Inference providers
docs.text:
Also known as: Together, Fireworks, Groq; OpenRouter

Companies that host open-weight models behind an API, often cheaper or faster than running them yourself. OpenRouter is an aggregator: one API that routes to many providers, closed and open.

Why it matters: The middle path between a frontier API and self-hosting.

Index aliases: Together / Fireworks / OpenRouter

docs.title: GPU kernel / Triton
docs.text:
A low-level program that runs on the GPU. FlashAttention is a kernel; Triton lets you write them in Python.

Why it matters: Where the big speed-ups come from; most engineers never write one, but the names come up.

Index aliases: Triton

docs.title: Serving on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Also known as: GPU node pools, KServe, vLLM on GKE

Running inference engines as containers on GPU nodes, with autoscaling and the usual K8s plumbing.

Why it matters: How a self-hosted model becomes a production service; the same platform skills you already have apply.

Index aliases: KServe / GKE GPU nodes

docs.title: Local inference stack
docs.text:
Also known as: llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio

Tools for running open-weight models on your own laptop or server.

Why it matters: The fastest way to try an open model: one command, no cloud, full privacy.

docs.title: Apple Silicon / MLX
docs.text:
Macs share memory between CPU and GPU, so a Mac with 64–512 GB of unified memory can run models that need several consumer GPUs; MLX is Apple's framework for it.

Why it matters: Why Mac laptops are popular for local LLMs despite having no NVIDIA GPU.

Index aliases: MLX

docs.title: Experiment tracking
docs.text:
Also known as: Weights & Biases, MLflow

Tools that log every training run's settings, loss curves and results.

Why it matters: How teams compare hundreds of runs without losing track of what worked.

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text:
Also known as: Jupyter, Colab, Kaggle

Interactive Python environments; Colab and Kaggle give free GPU time.

Why it matters: Where most tutorials (and Raschka's code) run; the cheapest way to get a GPU for an hour.

Index aliases: Colab / Kaggle

docs.title: 14. Beyond text: vision, audio, video
docs.text:
Cross-cutting: terms from image, speech and video AI that appear in general AI videos

The same building blocks (Transformers, embeddings, diffusion) applied to pixels and sound. Most of these live in the Generative AI box of Map 1, outside the LLM pipeline.

How to read this section

Each entry is a short definition followed by a Why it matters line that says, in plain words, what the idea buys you. Terms marked ★ belong to the 30 to learn first. The Also known as line lists the acronyms and other names you may hear in videos; all of them appear in the A–Z index.

docs.title: CLIP
docs.text:
Also known as: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training

A pair of encoders (image and text) trained so matching image–caption pairs get similar embeddings.

Why it matters: Lets you search images with words and is the glue inside most image generators and vision-language models.

docs.title: Vision-Language Model (VLM)
docs.text:
An LLM with a vision encoder attached, so it can take images as input (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Qwen-VL, LLaVA).

Why it matters: Why you can paste a screenshot or a chart into a chat and ask about it.

Index aliases: VLM

docs.title: Vision encoder / image tokens
docs.text:
Images are cut into patches, encoded (usually by a ViT) and projected into the LLM's token space; a typical image becomes a few hundred to a few thousand tokens.

Why it matters: Images are billed and context-limited as tokens, just like text.

Index aliases: Image tokens

docs.title: Latent diffusion
docs.text:
Also known as: Stable Diffusion

Diffusion run in the compressed latent space of a VAE instead of on raw pixels.

Why it matters: Makes image generation many times cheaper, which is what put it on consumer GPUs.

docs.title: U-Net / Diffusion Transformer (DiT)
docs.text:
The denoising network inside a diffusion model: a U-Net in older models, a Transformer (DiT) in newer ones (Stable Diffusion 3, Flux, Sora).

Why it matters: Another case of "Transformers ate the architecture"; same scaling story as LLMs.

Index aliases: DiT, U-Net

docs.title: Text encoder / guidance scale (CFG)
docs.text:
The text model that turns the prompt into conditioning vectors, and the knob (classifier-free guidance) controlling how strictly the image follows the prompt.

Why it matters: Guidance scale is the image-generation equivalent of temperature: higher is more literal, lower is more creative.

Index aliases: CFG, Guidance scale

docs.title: ControlNet / image conditioning
docs.text:
Add-ons that steer image generation with a sketch, pose, depth map or edge map in addition to text.

Why it matters: Gives precise control over composition instead of hoping the prompt lands.

Index aliases: ControlNet

docs.title: Image LoRA / style fine-tunes
docs.text:
LoRA adapters trained on a few dozen images to teach a diffusion model a style, product or face.

Why it matters: The same LoRA idea from section 9, applied to images; the basis of the custom-model marketplaces.

docs.title: Inpainting, outpainting, img2img
docs.text:
Regenerating part of an image, extending beyond its borders, or transforming an existing image guided by a prompt.

Why it matters: The editing operations behind "generative fill" features.

Index aliases: Inpainting, img2img

docs.title: Automatic Speech Recognition
docs.text:
Also known as: ASR, Whisper

Speech to text. Whisper is the widely used open model.

Why it matters: The first step of every voice assistant and the way meeting transcripts are made.

docs.title: Text-to-Speech / voice cloning (TTS)
docs.text:
Generating natural speech from text; cloning reproduces a specific voice from a short sample.

Why it matters: The output side of voice assistants, audiobooks and dubbing; cloning is also why voice-based fraud is rising.

Index aliases: TTS, Voice cloning

docs.title: Speech-to-speech / realtime models
docs.text:
Models that take audio in and produce audio out directly, with low latency, instead of chaining ASR → LLM → TTS.

Why it matters: Makes natural, interruptible voice conversation possible.

Index aliases: Realtime voice models

docs.title: Omni models
docs.text:
Single models trained on text, images, audio and video as input, producing text and speech (and sometimes images) as output.

Why it matters: Where the frontier is heading: one model for every modality instead of a pipeline of specialists.

Index aliases: Omni model

docs.title: Text-to-video
docs.text:
Also known as: Veo, Runway, Kling; OpenAI's Sora, discontinued in 2026

Diffusion or transformer models that generate video clips from a prompt or an image.

Why it matters: Same ideas as image generation, far more compute; the current showcase of generative AI, and a crowded market.

Index aliases: Sora, Veo / Runway

docs.title: World models
docs.text:
Models that learn to predict how an environment evolves (the next frame, the result of an action), used in robotics and games.

Why it matters: The argument that video generation is a step toward models that understand physics and planning.

Index aliases: World model

docs.title: OCR / document AI
docs.text:
Extracting text and structure from scanned documents and PDFs; increasingly done by VLMs directly.

Why it matters: How invoices, forms and old archives get into RAG pipelines.

Index aliases: Document AI

docs.title: Multimodal embeddings
docs.text:
Embedding models that map images, text and audio into one shared vector space.

Why it matters: Search a photo library with a sentence, or a product catalogue with a picture.

docs.title: Deepfake / synthetic media detection
docs.text:
Generated images, voices and videos impersonating real people, and the tools that try to detect or watermark them.

Why it matters: The main misuse of generative media; provenance standards (C2PA) and watermarks are the response.

Index aliases: Deepfake, C2PA / watermarking

docs.title: The Stanford CME295 slide, decoded
docs.text: The 35 acronyms from the “…but don’t worry!” slide of Stanford CME295 Transformers & LLMs (Autumn 2026, Lecture 1), each explained in plain words, grouped exactly as on the slide. Two groups describe what is inside the model, two describe how its weights are changed after pre-training, two describe how it is measured.

docs.title: Attention techniques
docs.text:
How a token looks at the other tokens. All six are variations on the same mechanism; the newer ones exist to cut memory and cost, not to change what attention does.

Inside the model (field guide section 6, Map 5)

docs.title: MHA — Multi-Head Attention
docs.text:
Attention is the part of a Transformer that lets each word look at the other words in the text and decide which ones matter for understanding it. When the model reads the word "it", attention is how it works out that "it" refers to "the cat" ten words earlier. "Multi-head" means the model does this looking-around several times in parallel, and each parallel copy, called a head, is free to look for a different kind of relationship. One head may track grammar, another the topic, another which words are close together. The results of all heads are glued back together before the next layer.

This is the original design from the 2017 "Attention Is All You Need" paper, and it is the baseline that every other technique in this box is compared against. GPT-2 small has 12 heads per layer; Llama-3-8B has 32.

Good to know: The catch: while the model generates text, it keeps a memory of every earlier token for every head (the KV cache). With many heads and long texts that memory becomes the thing that limits how many users fit on one GPU, which is exactly what GQA, MQA and MLA were invented to fix. — in the glossary

docs.title: GQA — Grouped-Query Attention
docs.text:
The memory problem of multi-head attention comes from every head keeping its own private copy of the "keys and values" of all earlier tokens. GQA keeps all the heads that ask questions (the queries) but makes several of them share one copy of the keys and values, like a group of readers sharing one copy of a book instead of each buying their own. The heads still look for different things; they just read from a shared memory.

The saving is large and the quality loss is almost nil. In Llama-3-8B, 32 query heads share 8 sets of keys and values, so the memory per token drops four times. That is what allows longer contexts and more simultaneous users on the same hardware.

Good to know: Introduced by Google researchers in 2023. It sits exactly between the original design (every head has its own memory) and MQA below (everyone shares a single memory). Nearly every model released since 2024 uses it: Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma. — in the glossary

docs.title: MQA — Multi-Query Attention
docs.text:
The extreme version of sharing: all the query heads share one single set of keys and values. The per-token memory shrinks by the number of heads, 32 times for a 32-head model, so generating text becomes very fast and cheap.

The price is quality. Every head now reads from the same, less rich memory, so the model loses some of its ability to track several relationships at once, and training was found to be less stable. That is why GQA, which shares among groups of heads rather than among all of them, became the standard compromise.

Good to know: Proposed by Noam Shazeer in 2019 with the memorable title "One Write-Head is All You Need". Used in Google's PaLM, in Falcon-7B and in the StarCoder code models. — in the glossary

docs.title: MLA — Multi-head Latent Attention
docs.text:
DeepSeek's answer to the same memory problem, taken from a different angle. Instead of making heads share their memory, MLA compresses the memory itself: for every token it stores a small, squeezed summary of the keys and values, like a zip file, and unpacks it on the fly whenever attention needs it. The squeezing is learned during training, so very little information is lost.

Because the stored summary is much smaller than the original keys and values, the saving is bigger than with GQA, and DeepSeek reports no loss of quality, sometimes a small gain. This is one of the main reasons DeepSeek's models can serve long conversations so cheaply.

Good to know: Introduced with DeepSeek-V2 in 2024 and kept in DeepSeek-V3 and R1. Compared with its predecessor model, DeepSeek reported a memory for past tokens about 93% smaller. One subtlety: the position information (RoPE, see next box) does not survive the squeezing, so a small separate piece of each key carries it. — in the glossary

docs.title: SWA — Sliding-Window Attention
docs.text:
Normally every token may look at every earlier token, so the cost of attention grows with the square of the text length. Sliding-window attention lets each token look only at the last few thousand tokens, like reading with a window that slides along the page. Cost and memory then stop growing with the length of the text, and the memory of past tokens can be a fixed-size rolling buffer.

Information from further back is not lost entirely: each layer passes on what it saw, so a token in layer ten indirectly knows about things far outside its own window. The trade-off is weaker recall of very distant details, which is why modern models mix windowed layers with a few normal "see everything" layers. Gemma 2 alternates the two one-to-one; Gemma 3 uses five windowed layers for every full one; OpenAI's gpt-oss alternates them too.

Good to know: The idea comes from Longformer (2020) and was popularised by the original Mistral 7B, which used a window of about 4,000 tokens. A related trick called attention sinks keeps the first few tokens of the text permanently visible, because the model habitually parks its spare attention on them. — in the glossary

docs.title: AttnRes — Attention Residuals
docs.text:
To understand this one you need the "residual stream": in a Transformer, every layer adds its output to a running total that is passed upward, so by the time the last layer runs it sees the sum of everything the earlier layers produced, each counted with equal weight. That fixed "add everything equally" rule has been unchanged since 2015.

AttnRes replaces it with a choice. Each layer learns how much to take from each earlier layer, using the same attention idea but applied across the depth of the network rather than across the words of the text. A later layer can lean heavily on layer three and ignore layer seven if that works better.

Good to know: Published by Moonshot AI (the Kimi lab) in March 2026. The gain is small but consistent across benchmarks, for roughly 4% extra training cost and 2% extra inference cost. Its main lesson for a learner: even the basic plumbing of the Transformer is still being redesigned in 2026. — in the glossary

docs.title: Architecture optimizations
docs.text:
Changes to the other parts of the Transformer block: how experts are routed, how position is encoded, how numbers are kept in a healthy range, and what the feed-forward layer looks like.

Inside the model (field guide sections 4 and 6, Map 5)

docs.title: MoE — Mixture of Experts
docs.text:
Each Transformer block contains a feed-forward network, the part that holds most of the model's stored knowledge. In a normal ("dense") model every token goes through the same one. In a Mixture of Experts, that single network is replaced by many smaller ones, the experts, plus a tiny router that sends each token to only a few of them. Think of a hospital reception sending each patient to two relevant specialists rather than to every doctor in the building.

The result is a model that holds far more knowledge in total while doing only the work of a much smaller model for each token. The names tell you both numbers: Qwen3-235B-A22B has 235 billion parameters in total but uses only 22 billion per token; DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion total and 37 billion active; Mixtral 8x7B picks 2 of its 8 experts. Most frontier models since 2025 are built this way.

Good to know: The costs: all the experts must sit in memory even though only a few run at a time, the router has to be trained so that work is spread evenly instead of everyone crowding the same two experts, and spreading experts across many GPUs is an engineering job of its own. — in the glossary

docs.title: RoPE — Rotary Positional Embedding
docs.text:
Attention on its own is blind to word order: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical to it. Position has to be injected somehow. RoPE does it by treating a token's position as an angle and rotating its query and key vectors by that angle, like turning the hands of a clock. When two rotated vectors are compared, only the difference between their angles matters, so attention naturally sees how far apart two words are rather than where exactly each one sits.

This has no learned parameters and works well, which is why nearly every current open model uses it: Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek. It is applied inside every attention layer, not once at the start.

Good to know: Introduced in 2021. One thing to know: a model trained on, say, 8,000-token texts does not automatically cope with 100,000-token texts; RoPE on its own extrapolates badly. Long contexts come from "stretching" tricks with names like position interpolation and YaRN, plus a short extra round of training. Llama 3 also turned up RoPE's internal base frequency, from 10,000 to 500,000, to make long contexts work. — in the glossary

docs.title: ALiBi — Attention with Linear Biases
docs.text:
A different answer to the word-order problem. Instead of encoding positions at all, ALiBi simply makes attention pay less to tokens that are further away by subtracting a penalty that grows with distance: nearby words matter a lot, far-away words a little. Each head uses a different steepness, so some heads stay very local and others look far.

Its selling point was "train short, test long": a model trained on short texts keeps working on much longer ones, because the rule is the same at every distance. It is also trivially cheap, with no extra parameters.

Good to know: Proposed in 2021 and used by the BLOOM and MPT models. In the end RoPE won the popularity contest: it scored better at large scale and fitted the fast attention software (FlashAttention) more easily. You will still meet ALiBi in papers and in older open models. — in the glossary

docs.title: LN — Layer Normalization
docs.text:
Deep networks break when the numbers flowing through them drift to huge or tiny values. LayerNorm fixes this by rescaling each token's vector so that its values have a standard spread, like converting every exam to a 0-to-100 scale before comparing them, and then letting the model stretch and shift the result with two learned knobs.

In a Transformer it sits just before each attention and each feed-forward sub-layer. Placing it before rather than after (the "pre-norm" layout, adopted from GPT-2 onwards) is what made 100-layer models trainable without constant crashes.

Good to know: Invented in 2016. Most current models use a lighter variant called RMSNorm (2019), which skips one of the steps and runs a bit faster with the same effect; Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek and Gemma all use it. When a slide says LN, RMSNorm or "norm layers", it is this idea. — in the glossary

docs.title: QKNorm — Query-Key Normalization
docs.text:
A targeted version of the same idea, applied at one specific spot: the query and key vectors are normalised right before they are compared inside attention. Why there? As models grow, those comparison scores can grow enormous, the attention softmax turns into a rigid "look at one token only", and training suddenly diverges with a loss spike.

With QK-Norm the scores stay in a bounded range, the spikes disappear, and the model can be trained with a higher learning rate, which means faster and cheaper training.

Good to know: First proposed in 2020, it became standard after Google's 22-billion-parameter vision Transformer (2023) used it to cure exactly this instability. Used in Gemma 3, OLMo 2 and Qwen3, and in many models released since. It works alongside RoPE: normalise first, then rotate. — in the glossary

docs.title: SwiGLU — Swish-Gated Linear Unit
docs.text:
The feed-forward network inside each block is where most of the parameters and most of the stored knowledge live. The classic version is "transform, then squash": multiply by a matrix, apply a simple activation function, multiply by another matrix. SwiGLU is a better-performing design: it runs two transforms in parallel and uses one of them as a gate that decides how much of the other passes through, like a valve on each signal line.

In practice it trains to a lower loss than the plain version for the same compute, which is why PaLM, Llama, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek all use it. The gating needs a third matrix, half again as many weights at the same width, so models make the hidden layer narrower to compensate.

Good to know: Proposed by Noam Shazeer in 2020 (the same person behind MQA). Gemma uses a cousin called GeGLU with a different activation; GPT-2 uses the old ungated design with a GELU activation, which is what Raschka's book implements. — in the glossary

docs.title: Model tuning
docs.text:
Changing the weights of an existing model with ordinary supervised training. SFT and DPO are done by labs and by you; PEFT, LoRA and QLoRA are the techniques that make it affordable on one GPU.

Stages 4 and 5 of Map 2 (field guide sections 8 and 9)

docs.title: SFT — Supervised Fine-Tuning
docs.text:
Show the model many examples of a prompt together with the ideal answer, and train it to reproduce those answers. A freshly pre-trained model only knows how to continue text; SFT is how it learns to follow instructions, answer a question instead of continuing it, use the chat format and stop when it is done. It is also how you teach a model your own format, tone or domain conventions.

Under the hood it is the same training loop as pre-training, just on a much smaller and hand-picked dataset, and usually with the loss computed only on the answer part, not on the prompt. Because the model copies what it sees, the quality of the examples matters far more than their number: a few thousand good ones are often enough, and bad examples are copied just as faithfully.

Good to know: It was step one of the InstructGPT recipe (2022) that led to ChatGPT. Famous datasets include Alpaca (52,000 examples generated by a stronger model) and ShareGPT (real conversations). It is also the mechanism of distillation: fine-tune a small model on a big model's answers. Raschka's chapter 7 is an SFT run. — in the glossary

docs.title: PEFT — Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
docs.text:
Fine-tuning all 8 billion weights of a model needs a lot of GPU memory, because for every weight the optimizer also stores extra bookkeeping numbers, and it produces a whole new 16-gigabyte copy of the model. PEFT is the family of methods that freeze the original model and train only a small add-on, often under 1% of the size, like patching a program instead of recompiling it.

What you gain: far less memory, faster training, the original stays intact, and you can keep dozens of small task-specific add-ons next to one base model and swap them in and out. Serving systems can even host hundreds of such add-ons at once.

Good to know: Members of the family: adapters (small extra layers inserted in each block, 2019), prompt tuning (learned vectors stuck in front of the input) and prefix tuning (learned vectors stuck in front of every layer), both from 2021, and LoRA (2021), which won. The Hugging Face library that implements them is literally called peft. — in the glossary

docs.title: LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation
docs.text:
The most popular PEFT method. Rather than changing a big weight matrix directly, LoRA learns a thin "patch" made of two small matrices whose product is added on top of the original. The patch has a tiny fraction of the numbers in the original matrix, yet it captures most of what a full fine-tune would have learned, because the change needed to adapt a model turns out to be simple.

The patch starts at zero, so training begins exactly from the base model and moves away from it gradually. It is usually applied to the attention matrices and often to the feed-forward ones too. The main knob is the rank, which sets the patch size; values between 8 and 64 are typical. At the end you can either keep the patch as a separate small file, or merge it into the base weights so inference costs nothing extra.

Good to know: Published by Microsoft researchers in 2021. For Llama-3-8B with a typical setup, the patch is about 42 million trainable numbers, roughly half a percent of the model, and an adapter file of under 100 megabytes. — in the glossary

docs.title: QLoRA — Quantized LoRA
docs.text:
LoRA on top of a compressed base model. The big frozen model is stored in 4-bit numbers, a quarter of the usual memory, while the small LoRA patch is trained in normal precision. When the model runs, the compressed weights are expanded on the fly, so the maths is the same; only the storage is smaller.

This is what lets a 65-to-70-billion-parameter model be fine-tuned on a single 48-gigabyte GPU, and a 7-to-13-billion model on an ordinary gaming card. The authors showed the results match full-precision fine-tuning almost exactly.

Good to know: Published in 2023. Three tricks make it work: a 4-bit number format designed for the typical shape of weight values, compressing the compression tables themselves, and shuffling optimizer memory to the CPU when there is a spike. It is the reason "fine-tune it yourself" became realistic for individuals. — in the glossary

docs.title: DPO — Direct Preference Optimization
docs.text:
A way to teach a model from preferences, pairs of answers where one is marked better than the other, without the full reinforcement-learning machinery of RLHF. DPO turns each pair into a simple training objective: raise the probability of the preferred answer, lower the probability of the rejected one, while staying close to the starting model so it does not drift.

You get most of the benefit of RLHF with a fraction of the complexity: no reward model to train, no sampling loop, only two models in memory instead of four. That is why open-model teams use it so widely; Zephyr, Tülu and Meta's Llama 3 pipeline all use it.

Good to know: Published by Stanford researchers in 2023. Its clever bit is mathematical: the authors showed that the RLHF objective has a closed-form answer, so the reward model can be eliminated. Note that the slide puts DPO under "model tuning", not under RL, precisely because no reinforcement-learning loop runs. Variants you may hear of: IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO. — in the glossary

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
Training by trial and reward instead of by example: the model produces answers, something scores them, and the weights move toward higher scores. This is how models learn to be preferred by people and, more recently, how they learn to reason.

Stage 4 of Map 2 (field guide section 8)

docs.title: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
docs.text:
The recipe behind ChatGPT. It has three stages. First, people compare pairs of model answers and say which is better. Second, a separate "judge" model, the reward model, is trained to predict those human preferences. Third, the language model practises on thousands of prompts: it writes answers, the judge scores them, and the weights are nudged toward answers that score higher, while a leash keeps the model close to its starting point so it does not drift into nonsense that happens to please the judge.

Examples alone (SFT) can teach a model the format of being helpful; RLHF teaches it what people actually prefer, which is how answers became more helpful, more polite and more careful. It is also where a model's "personality" is largely shaped.

Good to know: The ideas date from 2017 and were applied to language models from 2019; the InstructGPT paper (2022) is the canonical description. The expensive part is the practice stage, which needs four models in memory at once, and that cost is what DPO and GRPO were designed to cut. — in the glossary

docs.title: RLVR — Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
docs.text:
The same practice loop as RLHF, but with the human-trained judge replaced by an automatic check: did the maths answer match, do the unit tests pass, is the output in the required format. Because a unit test cannot be flattered or fooled, the model can be pushed much further than human preferences allow.

This is the main ingredient that produced the current reasoning models. When only correct answers are rewarded, the model discovers on its own that writing out long chains of reasoning before answering leads to more correct answers, and that behaviour grows during training. The limit is obvious: it only works where answers can be verified, so maths and code lead the way and the research question is how to extend it to softer tasks.

Good to know: The name was coined by the Allen Institute's Tülu 3 project in late 2024; DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) made it famous, training with simple rule-based rewards for correctness and format, using the GRPO algorithm below. — in the glossary

docs.title: RM — Reward Model
docs.text:
The trained judge used in RLHF. It takes a prompt and a candidate answer and outputs a single number: how good this answer is. It is built by taking a copy of the language model, replacing its text-producing head with a scoring head, and training it on the human comparison data. Once it exists, the practice loop can run millions of times without a human in the room.

Its weaknesses become the main model's weaknesses. If the judge has learned that long, confident answers tend to win votes, the trained model becomes long and confident whether or not it is right; this is called reward hacking, and it is why RLHF keeps a leash on the model and why RLVR replaces the judge with a verifier wherever it can.

Good to know: Two flavours you will hear about: an outcome reward model scores only the final answer, a process reward model scores each step of the reasoning. Using a general language model as the judge ("LLM-as-a-judge", in the metrics box) is the same idea without special training. — in the glossary

docs.title: PPO — Proximal Policy Optimization
docs.text:
The reinforcement-learning algorithm classically used inside RLHF. Its one big idea is caution. After seeing how the judge scored a batch of answers, it moves the model a little in the right direction, but it clips any update that would change the model's behaviour too much in one step. Plain reinforcement learning without that clipping tends to spiral out of control; PPO stays stable.

To decide how good each situation is, PPO trains an extra helper model, the "value" network, alongside the main one. Together with the reference model and the reward model, that makes four large models in memory during training, which is PPO's main drawback in the LLM setting.

Good to know: Published by OpenAI in 2017 for games and robotics, and reused for language models from 2019. In RLHF each generated token is treated as one "action", and the score arrives only when the answer is complete. — in the glossary

docs.title: GRPO — Group Relative Policy Optimization
docs.text:
A cheaper cousin of PPO from DeepSeek. For each question the model writes a group of answers, say sixteen. Each answer is scored, and its training signal is simply how much better or worse it did than its siblings in the group: above the group average means "do more of this", below means "do less". Because answers are judged relative to each other, PPO's extra value network is not needed at all.

That halves the memory and simplifies the whole setup, and it works with any kind of score: a reward model or an automatic check. It is the algorithm that trained DeepSeek-R1's reasoning and it spread through the open-source world within weeks.

Good to know: Published in DeepSeekMath in February 2024, a year before R1 made it famous. Known weaknesses: a bias toward longer answers, fixed in later variants, and instability on very long answers and on Mixture-of-Experts models, which led to GSPO. — in the glossary

docs.title: GSPO — Group Sequence Policy Optimization
docs.text:
Qwen's 2025 refinement of GRPO. GRPO judges and clips the update token by token. On very long answers those thousands of tiny per-token judgements add up a lot of noise, and on Mixture-of-Experts models, where slightly different experts may fire from one version of the model to the next, training could collapse altogether. GSPO judges and clips the whole answer as one unit instead.

The benefit is stable, efficient training at large scale with less engineering trickery: Qwen's team had needed a workaround called "routing replay" to keep GRPO working on their MoE models, and GSPO removed the need for it.

Good to know: Published by the Qwen team in July 2025 and used to train the Qwen3 Instruct, Coder and Thinking models. Implementations exist in the common open-source RL libraries (TRL, verl). — in the glossary

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Fixed exams used to compare models. Each is a dataset plus a scoring rule; the five on the slide cover maths, broad knowledge, expert science, real software engineering and the current "hardest exam".

Cross-cutting (field guide section 12)

docs.title: AIME — American Invitational Mathematics Examination
docs.text:
A real competition exam for strong US high-school students: 15 problems per paper, each with a whole-number answer between 0 and 999, no multiple choice to guess from, about three hours for a human. It became the favourite test for reasoning models because the answers are unambiguous and the problems need several steps of real mathematics, not recall.

The numbers tell the story of 2024–25. GPT-4-class models solved roughly one problem in ten on the 2024 paper. OpenAI's o1 and DeepSeek-R1 solved about four in five. Within another year, reasoning models were above 90%. The 2025 paper is popular precisely because it appeared after most models' training data was collected, so they cannot have memorised it.

Good to know: Scores are usually reported as single-attempt accuracy, often averaged over many tries; you will also see "cons@64", meaning the model answers 64 times and the most common answer counts. With only 30 problems a year, small score differences are noise. — in the glossary

docs.title: HLE — Humanity's Last Exam
docs.text:
A deliberately brutal exam built in early 2025 because the older benchmarks had become too easy. About 2,500 questions were written by subject experts across more than a hundred fields, from maths and physics to law, linguistics and classics, and only questions that the best models at the time got wrong were kept. Roughly one in seven needs an image as well as text.

The name is the point: it is meant to be the last academic-style benchmark worth building. When models pass it, exams of this kind stop telling us anything. At launch the best models scored in the single digits; with reasoning and web tools, scores climbed into the tens of percent during 2025 and 2026.

Good to know: Created by the Center for AI Safety together with Scale AI, with nearly a thousand contributors. Besides accuracy it reports how well calibrated a model is, so a model that is confidently wrong is penalised. — in the glossary

docs.title: MMLU — Massive Multitask Language Understanding
docs.text:
The classic general-knowledge test: around 14,000 four-option multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, from elementary maths to law, medicine and history. From 2021 to 2024 it was the headline number in nearly every model announcement, usually run "5-shot", with five worked examples shown first.

Top models now score around 90%, so it mostly tells you that a model is not bad rather than how good it is. A few percent of its questions are known to be wrong, and many of them have leaked into training data. For separating strong models, the harder MMLU-Pro (2024) took over: 12,000 questions, ten options instead of four, more reasoning required, which knocks 16 to 33 points off the scores.

Good to know: Published in 2020 by Dan Hendrycks and colleagues. When a 2026 lecture mentions MMLU, it is usually as the example of a benchmark that got saturated. — in the glossary

docs.title: SWE-bench — Software Engineering Benchmark
docs.text:
The benchmark for coding agents, and the one most relevant to your work. Take real bug reports and feature requests from popular open-source Python projects (Django, scikit-learn, sympy and others), give the model the repository, and check whether its patch makes the project's own tests pass while not breaking the ones that passed before. It measures finishing a real engineering job, not writing a function from a description.

Scores went from almost nothing in 2023 to well over half the tasks in 2025, the clearest single sign of the agentic-coding shift. The number labs quote is SWE-bench Verified, a subset of 500 tasks that human reviewers checked are actually solvable; the full set has about 2,300 tasks, and a cheap 300-task "Lite" version exists.

Good to know: Published by Princeton researchers in 2023; the Verified subset was curated by OpenAI in 2024. One caveat to keep in mind: the result depends as much on the agent scaffolding around the model as on the model itself. — in the glossary

docs.title: GPQA — Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A
docs.text:
Hard science questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by people with PhDs in those fields, designed so that a smart person outside the field, given unlimited time and Google, still gets only about a third right. Experts in the same field get about two thirds. It tests deep expertise rather than memorised trivia, hence "Google-proof".

The number usually quoted is GPQA Diamond, the subset of 198 questions that experts answered correctly and non-experts mostly missed. GPT-4 scored around 39% when the test came out in 2023; reasoning models passed 80% in 2025, so it is approaching the point where it stops being useful.

Good to know: Four options per question means pure guessing already gives 25%, worth remembering when two models are a couple of points apart. — in the glossary

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The numbers you compute. A benchmark is a dataset; a metric is how you score it, or how you measure something that is not a benchmark at all, like speed or how far a model has drifted.

Spread across the lifecycle: pre-training (PPL), post-training (KL), inference (TTFT, TPOT), applications (LaaJ), evaluation (Pass@k, Elo)

docs.title: PPL — Perplexity
docs.text:
How surprised a language model is by a piece of text. A perplexity of 20 means that, on average, the model was as uncertain about each next token as if it were choosing among 20 equally likely options. Lower is better. It is computed directly from the training loss, which is why it is the number labs watch fall during pre-training and the standard way to compare models on raw text.

It measures prediction, not helpfulness: a model can have excellent perplexity and still be a poor assistant. It also depends on the tokenizer and on the text used, so you can only compare models that share a tokenizer, on the same data.

Good to know: For scale: GPT-2 small scores about 37 on a standard Wikipedia test set, the largest GPT-2 about 17. Raschka's chapter 5 prints it during training, and it is the quick check people run after compressing a model to 4 bits: if perplexity barely moved, the compression did little harm. — in the glossary

docs.title: LaaJ — LLM-as-a-Judge
docs.text:
Using a strong language model to grade another model's answers, either by giving a score against a rubric or by saying which of two answers is better. It is far cheaper than human raters and agrees with them most of the time, so teams run it like a test suite on every change to a prompt or a model.

The judge has known biases: it prefers longer answers, it prefers whichever answer it sees first, it prefers its own writing style, and it is weak at checking maths. Good setups counter these by swapping the order of the two answers, giving the judge a reference solution, and using strict rubrics.

Good to know: The approach was formalised in 2023, when researchers showed that GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human preferences more than 80% of the time, about as often as humans agree with each other. The same idea doubles as a training signal (the reward in RLAIF) and as a filter for generated training data. Raschka's chapter 7 uses a local Llama model as the judge. — in the glossary

docs.title: KL — Kullback–Leibler divergence
docs.text:
A number that says how different two probability distributions are: zero when they are identical, growing as they diverge. In LLM training it is mostly used as a leash. During RLHF or GRPO the model is penalised for moving its token probabilities too far from the starting model, which stops it from degenerating into gibberish that happens to score well with the judge. The strength of that leash is a tuning knob, and DPO has the same knob built in.

It also appears in distillation, where a small student model is trained to match the full probability distribution of a big teacher rather than just copying its words, and in the maths behind the training loss itself: minimising cross-entropy is the same as minimising the KL divergence to the real text.

Good to know: Named after two statisticians from the 1950s. Note that it is one-directional: the divergence from A to B is not the same as from B to A, which is why papers are careful to say which way round they measure it. — in the glossary

docs.title: Pass@k — Pass at k
docs.text:
The chance that at least one of k attempts is correct. Pass@1 is what a user experiences on a single try. Pass@10 or pass@100 shows what the model can do if you let it try many times and pick the attempt that works, which is realistic for code (run the tests) and for anything with an automatic checker.

The gap between the two is informative. A big gap between pass@1 and pass@100 means the capability is in there but unreliable; reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often works by closing that gap, pulling single-try success up toward what many tries could already achieve.

Good to know: Introduced with OpenAI's Codex in 2021 together with a careful way of estimating it from many samples. It is standard on coding benchmarks (HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) and maths. Do not confuse it with majority voting, where the most common answer is chosen without any checker. — in the glossary

docs.title: Elo — Elo rating
docs.text:
A rating system borrowed from chess. On Chatbot Arena (now LMArena), people chat with two anonymous models side by side and vote for the better answer. Each vote moves the winner's rating up and the loser's down, more when the result was a surprise, and the ratings settle into a leaderboard. A 400-point gap means the higher-rated model is expected to win about ten times out of eleven.

It is the closest thing to "which model do people prefer", and it has the weaknesses of a popularity contest: longer and nicer-looking answers win votes, the prompts are skewed toward casual use, and votes can be gamed. The site added "style control", which corrects for length and formatting, and separate leaderboards for coding and hard prompts.

Good to know: Named after Arpad Elo, who designed it in the 1960s. LMArena stopped using the chess-style running update at the end of 2023 and now fits all votes together with a statistical model, but it still reports scores on the familiar Elo-like scale, with confidence intervals. — in the glossary

docs.title: TTFT — Time To First Token
docs.text:
How long the user waits before the first word of the answer appears, the pause you feel after pressing Enter. It is made of three parts: time in the queue on a busy server, the time to process the whole prompt (the "prefill" phase), and the network. Prompt processing dominates: it grows with the length of the prompt, so pasting a long document or stuffing many retrieved passages into the context makes it longer. A 100,000-token prompt can take several seconds even on a top GPU.

Two things make it feel fast. Prompt caching reuses the already-processed part of a prompt that repeats between requests, such as a long system prompt or the same document, and can cut TTFT many times over. Streaming does not change TTFT but makes the rest of the answer appear as it is generated instead of all at once.

Good to know: Product teams typically aim for well under a second for chat. If you benchmark a model API, this is one of the two numbers to record; the other is TPOT. — in the glossary

docs.title: TPOT — Time Per Output Token
docs.text:
Once the answer has started, how long each additional token takes; turn it upside down and you get the familiar tokens-per-second. Total waiting time is TTFT plus TPOT times the number of tokens in the answer, which is why long answers from a reasoning model feel slow even when the first token came fast.

What sets it is surprising: for each new token the model has to read all of its weights from GPU memory, and that reading, not the arithmetic, is the bottleneck. An 8-billion-parameter model in normal precision is 16 gigabytes; an H100 can read about 3,350 gigabytes per second; so one token can never take less than about 5 milliseconds, roughly 200 tokens per second for a single user. Compress the weights to 4 bits and the ceiling rises four times, which is why quantization speeds up generation. Speculative decoding, where a small model drafts several tokens and the big one checks them in one read, is the other main trick.

Good to know: Serving many users at once lets the server share one read of the weights across all of them, which is great for throughput but can make each individual user's TPOT a little worse. Typical values for hosted models are 10 to 50 milliseconds per token, that is 20 to 100 tokens per second. — in the glossary

docs.title: Map 1 — The big picture
docs.text:
Where AI, machine learning, deep learning and LLMs sit.

Each box is inside the one around it. LLMs sit in the overlap of two ideas: they are Transformers (an architecture) and they are generative (what they do). Everything in the LLM lifecycle lives inside that small blue box.

docs.title: Map 7 — Decision guide
docs.text:
Prompt, RAG, fine-tune, or train?

Start at the left column and move right only if the cheaper fix fails. Most real problems never leave the first column.

Symptom First try (hours) Then (days) Last resort (weeks+) Don't Wrong, outdated or missing factsDoesn't know your product, your docs, last week's data Put the facts in the prompt; add RAG or a search / DB tool Improve retrieval: chunking, hybrid search, reranker, citations Continued pre-training on your domain corpus (rare, expensive) Fine-tuning is a poor way to teach facts: it is unreliable and goes stale. Right content, wrong formWrong tone, format, length, language; ignores conventions Prompt engineering: explicit rules, few-shot examples, structured outputs LoRA fine-tune on a few hundred ideal examples Full fine-tune with thousands of examples Pre-training. Style is cheap to teach; knowledge is not. Can't do the task at allFails at multi-step reasoning, complex code, long planning Bigger or reasoning model; chain-of-thought; decompose into steps Agent with tools: let it run code, search, check its work RL fine-tuning with verifiable rewards on your task (research-grade) Expecting a 7B model to match a frontier model by prompting harder. Too slow or too expensiveLatency, token bill, GPU cost Shorter prompts, prompt caching, smaller model for easy requests (routing) Quantization, speculative decoding, better serving engine, batching Distill or fine-tune a small model to replace the big one on your task Adding more context "to be safe": cost grows with every token. Unreliable or unsafe outputsHallucinates, breaks JSON, follows injected instructions Structured outputs, validation, guardrails, grounding with citations Evals + LLM-as-judge in CI; human-in-the-loop for risky actions Fine-tune for refusal / format behaviour on your own red-team data Trusting a single model call for anything irreversible. Needs a new language or deep specialist knowledgeLow-resource language, dense legal / medical / scientific domain Pick a model already strong in it; RAG for the long tail Continued pre-training on a large domain corpus, then SFT Train from scratch Training from scratch unless you are a lab; it costs millions and the base models are better than you can make.

The rule of thumb. Prompting changes nothing and costs nothing: try it first. RAG adds knowledge. Fine-tuning changes behaviour (style, format, reliability on a narrow task) and is bad at adding knowledge. Continued pre-training adds deep knowledge but needs a corpus and real GPU time. Pre-training from scratch is for labs.

docs.title: Map 4 — Life of a request
docs.text:
What happens when you call a model.

One API call, from your code to the model and back. Steps 3–5 are the Transformer itself (Map 5); everything else is tokenization, sampling and plumbing. No weights change anywhere on this page.

docs.title: The steps in words
docs.text:
1. Your app assembles the prompt — system prompt + conversation history + retrieved docs (RAG) + tool definitions + the new user message. Everything the model will know about this request is in this text; nothing else exists for it. (Stage 7 — context engineering)
  2. Tokenizer: text → token IDs — "Katowice" → sub-word pieces → integer IDs. Polish costs about 2× the tokens of English. The prompt plus the maximum output must fit the context window. Billed as input tokens. (Stage 1)
  3. Embedding lookup (+ position) — token IDs → vectors of shape [T × d_model]. GPT-2 adds learned positions here; RoPE models add position inside each attention layer. (Stage 2)
  4. N × Transformer blocks: PREFILL — all prompt tokens are processed in parallel; attention reads the whole prompt and the keys and values are stored in the KV cache. Compute-bound; decides time-to-first-token. Prompt caching reuses this work for a repeated prefix.
  5. LM head → logits → softmax — one score for every token in the vocabulary (≈ 50k–200k) → probabilities that sum to 1. Logprobs come from here. A reasoning model's "thinking" is ordinary tokens produced the same way.
  6. Sampling: choose ONE token — temperature scales the logits; top-p / top-k cut the tail; repetition penalty; constrained decoding for JSON schemas. Temperature 0 ≈ always the top token. (Stage 6 — your knobs)
  7. Append it, run the blocks for that one token: DECODE — uses the KV cache, so only the new token is computed; repeat until EOS, max tokens or a stop sequence. Memory-bound; decides tokens per second. Reasoning models loop here for their thinking tokens before the visible answer. Speculative decoding and batching make this loop faster and cheaper.
  8. Detokenize → stream text back to your app — if the output is a tool call, your code runs it and the result goes back into the prompt → step 1 again (the agent loop). Billed as output tokens (3–8× the input price). (Stage 7)

Time to first token = steps 1–6 once. Tokens per second = how fast step 7 loops.

docs.title: Three things to remember
docs.text:
• Reading tip. A video about “training” is about stages 3–5. A video about “fine-tuning” is usually stage 5 (yours) but sometimes stage 4 (the lab’s). Anything about prompts, RAG, tools or agents is stage 7 and never touches the weights.
  • Three models, one lineage. Base model (after 3) → instruct / chat model (after 4) → your specialised model (after 5). Llama-3-8B is a base model; Llama-3-8B-Instruct has been through stage 4.
  • Same loop, different data. Stages 3, 4 and 5 all run the training loop of Map 3. What changes is the data (web text, human preferences, your examples), the scale, and who pays.

docs.title: Map 6 — RAG and the agent loop
docs.text:
Around the model.

Stage 7 in two pictures. Both use a frozen model; the engineering is in the pipeline. RAG gives the model your knowledge; the agent loop gives it hands. MCP is the plug between the loop and the tools.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
docs.text:
• What RAG buys you: knowledge the model never saw, kept current by re-indexing, with sources, and no training.
  • What usually goes wrong: retrieval, not generation. Tune chunking, use hybrid search and a reranker, and evaluate “did the right chunk come back?” separately from the answer.
  • Weights never change. The embedding model and the LLM are both frozen; all the work is in the pipeline around them.
  • Agentic RAG: instead of one fixed retrieve-then-answer pass, the agent below calls “search” as a tool, as many times as it needs, and decides when it has enough.

docs.title: The agent loop, with MCP
docs.text: The model answers once; the loop is yours. MCP standardises the arrow between the loop and the tools: one server, every client. A2A standardises agents calling other agents. See section 11 — Building applications.

docs.title: Map 3 — Neural-network foundations
docs.text:
The training loop and the architecture families.

Every neural network, from a 10-line PyTorch example to a frontier LLM, is trained with the same four-step loop. The architecture decides what happens inside step 1; the data decides what the loss compares against.

docs.title: What you turn, what you watch
docs.text: Knobs (hyperparameters) learning rate and its schedule · batch size · epochs / steps · model size (layers, width) · dropout · weight decay · LoRA rank · temperature (inference only) What you watch training loss going down · validation loss (if it rises while training loss keeps falling → overfitting) · gradient norm (spikes → lower the LR or clip) · perplexity · eval benchmarks What can go wrong overfitting · underfitting · vanishing or exploding gradients · loss spikes · catastrophic forgetting (fine-tuning) · reward hacking (RL) · data contamination (evals) Where the compute goes matrix multiplications in steps 1 and 3, run on GPUs in BF16 · memory is weights + gradients + optimizer state (≈ 16 bytes per parameter for full training with AdamW, ≈ 2 bytes for inference)

docs.title: Map 5 — Inside one Transformer block
docs.text:
With the real numbers.

Shapes are written as [B, T, d]: batch size, tokens in the sequence, vector width. GPT-2 small (124M) is the model Raschka builds in chapters 3–4; Llama-3-8B shows the same block with 2024 numbers. B = 1 and T = your prompt length at inference time.

docs.title: Two models, same block
docs.text: GPT-2 small (2019) Llama-3-8B (2024) Vocabulary 50,257 128,256 Context length (trained) 1,024 8,192 (3.1: 128k) d_model (hidden size) 768 4,096 Attention heads 12 × 64 32 × 128 (8 KV heads: GQA) Layers (blocks) 12 32 FFN hidden size 3,072 (GELU) 14,336 (SwiGLU) Normalization LayerNorm RMSNorm Position learned RoPE Parameters 124M 8.0B Weights file (BF16) 0.25 GB 16 GB

docs.title: Where GPT-2's 124M parameters are
docs.text: Embeddings ≈ 32% · attention ≈ 23% · feed-forward ≈ 45%. Token embedding 50,257 × 768 = 38.6M (shared with the LM head) · positions 1,024 × 768 = 0.8M · per block: attention 2.4M + FFN 4.7M = 7.1M, × 12 = 85M. In bigger models the embeddings shrink to a few percent and the FFN dominates, which is why MoE replaces the FFN.

docs.title: Why the shapes matter
docs.text:
• T appears squared only in the attention scores [B, h, T, T]. That is the quadratic cost of long context, and what FlashAttention, GQA and the KV cache attack.
  • The FFN never looks at other tokens. It is the same 768 → 3072 → 768 function applied to each position; attention is the only place tokens exchange information.
  • The residual stream is the [B, T, 768] vector that each block adds to. The LM head reads it only at the end.
  • Parameter count ≈ 12 × n_layers × d_model² for the blocks (+ embeddings). Double the width, four times the parameters.

docs.title: The three formulas worth memorising
docs.text:
• θ ← θ − η ∇_θ 𝓛 — gradient descent: move the weights a little downhill.
  • 𝓛 = −Σ log p_θ(x_t | x_<t) — next-token cross-entropy: be surprised as little as possible by the real text.
  • Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V — each token takes a weighted average of the others, weights from query–key similarity.

docs.title: Model families and how to read a model name
