docs.title: Decoding a model name
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct family · generation · parameter count · post-trained for chat Qwen3-235B-A22B 235B total parameters, 22B active per token: a Mixture of Experts Mixtral-8x7B 8 experts of ~7B each; ≈ 47B total, ≈ 13B active -Base / -Instruct / -Chat raw pre-trained model vs. post-trained assistant -R1, -Thinking, o1 / o3 reasoning model: thinks before answering -mini, -nano, -flash, -haiku, -lite the small, fast, cheap tier of a family -VL, -vision, -omni accepts images (and audio / video) -Coder, -Code trained or tuned for programming -Distill-, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B a small model trained to imitate a big one: teacher first (DeepSeek-R1), the small base model last (Qwen 7B) -Q4_K_M.gguf, -GPTQ, -AWQ, -FP8 quantized files: 4-bit GGUF for llama.cpp / Ollama, GPTQ / AWQ for GPUs, FP8 for H100s -128k, -1M context window -v0.3, -2507 revision or release date (July 2025) Dense vs MoE if no "A" number and no "x", it is probably dense: all parameters used for every token

Three lineages to keep apart: base → instruct → reasoning (same family, more post-training each step); dense vs MoE (all parameters vs a routed subset per token); full precision vs quantized file (same model, fewer bits).

docs.text:
• Start — Section 1 and Map 1: the vocabulary of the field and where LLMs sit.
  • Then — Section 2 and the paradigm table: supervised / self-supervised / RL are the three words that unlock everything else.
  • Core — Sections 4 → 5 → 6 with Maps 3 and 5: the training loop, tokens, the Transformer. This is Raschka chapters 2–4.
  • Lifecycle — Sections 7 → 8 → 9 with Map 2: pre-training, post-training, your fine-tuning. Raschka chapters 5–7.
  • Using it — Sections 10 → 11 with Maps 4, 6 and 7: inference, prompting, RAG, agents, MCP. Your day job.

docs.title: Software engineer's translation table
docs.text:
Every AI concept mapped to something you already run in production. The analogies are imperfect on purpose; the third column says where they break.

AI term Closest thing you know How it maps, and where it breaks Model (weights) A compiled binary / artifact You cannot read it; it was produced by a build (training) you probably did not run. Training The build pipeline Hours to weeks, expensive, produces one artifact. You rarely rebuild; you configure around the artifact. Inference Runtime / executing the binary Pure function of input + weights. No state change. Pre-training vs post-training Compiling the kernel vs. configuring the distro One is the giant general build; the other makes it usable for people. Fine-tuning (LoRA) A patch / plugin on the artifact Small diff on top of the original; swap it in and out. Prompt / system prompt Request payload + config file The system prompt is config that ships with your app; the user message is the request. Context window Max request size (plus response) Hard limit; everything you want the model to consider must fit. Tokens The billing and sizing unit Like bytes for storage: context limits, speed and price are all per token. Temperature A randomness / seed setting 0 = deterministic-ish; higher = more variety. Embeddings + vector DB An index for fuzzy, by-meaning lookup Like a search index, but similarity is semantic rather than keyword. RAG A DB lookup before the call Fetch relevant rows, put them in the request, then call the model. Tool use / function calling The model emitting a method call you execute The model returns {name, args}; your code runs it and returns the result. Agent A while-loop with function calls and a stop condition while not done: call model → maybe call tool → append result. MCP An interface spec (like OpenAPI / JDBC) for tools Implement the server once; any compliant client can call it. Hallucination A confident bug with no stack trace The output is well-formed and wrong. Validate, ground, test. Evals Your test suite Run on every prompt or model change; LLM-as-judge is a flaky-but-useful assertion. Observability / tracing Logs, metrics, traces Same tools (OpenTelemetry), same reasons. Prompt injection SQL injection for LLMs Untrusted input interpreted as instructions. Treat all retrieved content as data. Guardrails Input validation + output validation Schema checks, classifiers, allow-lists, around the model call. Model API vs self-hosting SaaS vs running it on your own GKE Same trade-offs: ops burden, cost at scale, data residency, control.

docs.title: Eight naming traps that confuse everyone
docs.text:
“Fine-tuning” means two things — Labs say it for post-training (SFT, RLHF) that turns a base model into a chat model. Engineers say it for adapting a finished model to their own task (LoRA). Same mechanics, different stage and budget.

“Training” vs “inference” — Training changes weights (stages 3–5). Inference only runs the frozen weights (stage 6). Prompting, RAG and agents never change weights; they are inference-time engineering (stage 7).

“Alignment” is both a goal and a stage — As a goal: the model behaves as intended. As a stage: the RLHF / DPO / safety part of post-training.

Model, weights, checkpoint, parameters — All the same thing from different angles: the learned numbers. A checkpoint is a saved copy; parameters count them; weights is the file you download.

Supervised vs self-supervised — Same loss, same loop. The difference is where the label comes from: a human (SFT) or the data itself (next token).

Agent vs model — A model answers once. An agent is a model in a loop with tools, memory and a stopping rule. The agent is code you write; the model is the thing it calls.

Embedding (the layer) vs embeddings (the API) — Inside an LLM, the embedding layer turns token IDs into vectors. An “embedding model” or embeddings API is a separate model that turns whole texts into vectors for search. Same idea, different object.

Context window vs memory — The context window is the model’s working memory for one request. “Memory” features are retrieval: facts stored outside and pasted back in. The model itself remembers nothing between calls.
